title: Myofascial pain in older adults: a geroscience-informed framework integrating precision geriatrics and digital therapeutics
authors: Chang Zhu; Jie Xu; Yating Gong; Chaoyu Wang; Wenting Xu; Lijun Chen
pain_condition_detail: Myofascial pain syndrome (MPS) in older adults, with reference to chronic low back pain and fibromyalgia.
bps_function_set: conclusion; explanatory framework; intervention rationale; justification; organizing principle; policy or practice implication
bps_operationalization_summary: The paper proposes a geroscience-informed BPS framework for geriatric MPS. It elaborates biological mechanisms (sarcopenia, inflammaging, central sensitization), mentions psychological constructs (catastrophizing, fear-avoidance, depression), and minimally addresses social factors (social isolation, family support). Integration is directional between bio and psych, but triadic integration is partial.
integration_mechanism_summary: The paper proposes that psychological factors (catastrophizing, anxiety, depression) directionally amplify central sensitization (bio-psych). Social factors are mentioned as outcomes or comorbidities but not mechanistically linked. Triadic integration is partial: the BPS definition includes bio and psych but omits social.
conceptual_tensions_1: The paper claims a biopsychosocial framework but defines it as bio-psych only, omitting social
conceptual_tensions_2: Biological domain is elaborated with multiple mechanisms, while social domain is minimal and not integrated
conceptual_tensions_3: The BPS label is used as an organizing principle and intervention rationale, but triadic integration is partial
additional_observations_1: The paper introduces geroscience as a new lens for MPS, but this is primarily biological, not biopsychosocial
additional_observations_2: Digital therapeutics are presented as a way to scale psychological interventions, but social barriers (digital divide) are acknowledged
additional_observations_3: The case example illustrates real-world gaps in multidisciplinary care, but the framework remains largely theoretical
synthesis_note: This narrative review proposes a geroscience-informed BPS framework for geriatric MPS. It elaborates biological mechanisms (sarcopenia, inflammaging, central sensitization) but treats psychological constructs as modulators without mechanistic depth. Social factors are minimally addressed. The BPS label is used as an organizing principle and intervention rationale, but triadic integration is partial: bio-psych integration is directional, while social is loosely attached. The paper contributes a geroscience lens but does not substantively operationalize the full BPS model.
coding_rationale: Typology is pseudo_bps because BPS language is used but social domain is minimal and triadic integration is partial. Bio-dominant balance reflects the elaborated biological content. Integration is directional for bio-psych, mentioned for others.

title: Myofascial pain in older adults: a geroscience-informed framework integrating precision geriatrics and digital therapeutics
authors: Chang Zhu; Jie Xu; Yating Gong; Chaoyu Wang; Wenting Xu; Lijun Chen
pain_condition_detail: Myofascial pain syndrome (MPS) in older adults; related chronic musculoskeletal pain and chronic low back pain.
context_note: Older adults in community, long-term care, primary/geriatric clinics, and Chinese/resource-limited settings; U.S. prevalence cited.
bps_function_set: background framing; explanatory framework; intervention rationale; organizing principle; policy or practice implication
bps_operationalization_summary: The model is operationalized as a clinician-facing review framework: age-specific pathophysiology, precision diagnostics, pharmacology/de-prescribing, non-pharmacological interventions, psychological therapies, and multidisciplinary care. It defines BPS pain as peripheral nociception, central processing, and psychological state, then maps interventions to those domains rather than testing a three-domain causal model.
integration_mechanism_summary: The strongest pathway is biological: aging-related tissue and inflammatory changes produce central sensitization, which psychological factors top-down modulate. Social factors mainly alter access to psychological care and multidisciplinary implementation; no full three-domain causal mechanism is specified.
conceptual_tensions_1: MPS is framed both as a localized myofascial condition with trigger points and as a complex geriatric syndrome rooted in aging biology
conceptual_tensions_2: The review advocates a geroscience-informed mechanistic cascade but states that interactions among aging mechanisms remain largely theoretical
conceptual_tensions_3: Digital therapeutics are promoted for access, while the digital divide is identified as a barrier to equitable uptake
conceptual_tensions_4: Multidisciplinary care is idealized, but the case example shows missing psychology and social work in China/resource-limited settings
conceptual_tensions_5: Non-pharmacological care is prioritized, but pharmacological precision prescribing and de-prescribing remain necessary
additional_observations_1: The review prioritizes high-quality evidence but uses a narrative thematic synthesis, not a pooled meta-analysis or formal systematic review
additional_observations_2: The social domain is mostly implementation/access: digital divide, family support, social determinants, and care-team composition
additional_observations_3: The clinical case is used rhetorically and illustratively, not analyzed as empirical data
additional_observations_4: Several citation placeholders are blank in the supplied text, so attribution is sometimes unresolvable
additional_observations_5: The framework is actionable for clinicians but not empirically validated as a model
synthesis_note: This narrative review operationalizes BPS as a clinician-facing multimodal framework for geriatric MPS. Biological geroscience mechanisms are the strongest thread; psychological constructs and therapies are integrated mechanistically with central sensitization; social factors enter mainly as access, support, and care-system gaps. It offers descriptive triadic integration but few tested cross-domain pathways.
coding_rationale: Biological and psychological content are elaborated; social content is mentioned. Bio-psych integration is mechanistic, triadic integration descriptive. Typology true_integrative despite thin social domain.
biological_factors_01_factor_verbatim: Sarcopenia, the age-related loss of skeletal muscle mass and strength, is a cornerstone of this decline. Beginning in the fourth decade of life, muscle mass decreases by approximately 8% per decade, accelerating after the age of 70. In MPS, sarcopenia creates a vulnerable substrate.
biological_factors_02_factor_verbatim: This leads to fascial stiffening, reduced tissue compliance, and impaired gliding between fascial layers. This increased stiffness can directly contribute to pain by compressing embedded nociceptors and small nerve fibers.
biological_factors_03_factor_verbatim: Underpinning these changes is profound mitochondrial dysfunction. Aging muscle is characterized by a decline in mitochondrial biogenesis, reduced efficiency of the electron transport chain, and an accumulation of mitochondrial DNA mutations.
biological_factors_04_factor_verbatim: Superimposed on these structural changes is a systemic, pro-inflammatory state known as “inflammaging.” This refers to the chronic, low-grade, sterile inflammation that characterizes the aging process.
biological_factors_05_factor_label: cellular senescence and the senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP)
biological_factors_05_factor_verbatim: A key driver of inflammaging is cellular senescence—the accumulation of non-dividing but metabolically active cells that secrete a cocktail of inflammatory mediators, known as the senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP).
biological_factors_06_factor_verbatim: In many older adults with chronic MPS, the pain experience is no longer solely driven by the peripheral MTrP. The constant barrage of nociceptive signals from the dysfunctional muscle tissue leads to profound neuroplastic changes in the central nervous system (CNS), a process known as central sensitization.
biological_factors_07_factor_label: neuroendocrine dysregulation and the HPA axis
biological_factors_07_factor_verbatim: Age-related changes in the neuroendocrine system also play a crucial role. Dysregulation of the hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenal (HPA) axis, the body’s central stress response system, is common in older adults.
biological_factors_08_factor_verbatim: For instance, a high prevalence of vitamin D deficiency has been observed in patients with chronic MPS, with age and limited sun exposure being significant risk factors.
biological_factors_09_factor_verbatim: Non-Steroidal Anti-Inflammatory Drugs (NSAIDs): While effective for acute inflammatory pain, the chronic use of NSAIDs (e.g., ibuprofen, naproxen) is strongly discouraged in the elderly.
biological_factors_10_factor_verbatim: Gabapentinoids (Gabapentin and Pregabalin): These drugs are widely prescribed for neuropathic pain, but their efficacy in nociceptive or mixed pain states like MPS is limited.
biological_factors_11_factor_verbatim: Selective Sodium Channel Blockers: A highly promising frontier is the development of selective inhibitors of the NaV1.8 sodium channel.
biological_factors_12_factor_verbatim: A pharmacological frontier with particular relevance to geriatric MPS is senolytic therapy—agents designed to selectively eliminate senescent cells that accumulate with aging and drive chronic inflammation through the senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP).

title: Myofascial pain in older adults: a geroscience-informed framework integrating precision geriatrics and digital therapeutics
authors: Chang Zhu; Jie Xu; Yating Gong; Chaoyu Wang; Wenting Xu; Lijun Chen
pain_condition_detail: Myofascial pain syndrome in older adults
context_note: International perspective with reference to Chinese healthcare system limitations
bps_function_set: background framing; explanatory framework; organizing principle; policy or practice implication
bps_operationalization_summary: The review uses BPS as an organizing principle to structure a geroscience-informed framework for geriatric MPS management, integrating biological aging mechanisms, psychological therapies, and social care coordination without specifying detailed cross-domain pathways.
integration_mechanism_summary: The paper proposes that biological aging mechanisms (sarcopenia, inflammaging, cellular senescence) drive MPS pathophysiology, which is amplified by psychological factors (catastrophizing, anxiety, depression) through central sensitization. Social integration occurs through multidisciplinary team coordination, but explicit biological-social pathways are not specified.
conceptual_tensions_1: Tension between theoretical integration of aging mechanisms and practical clinical implementation
conceptual_tensions_2: Tension between digital therapeutics promise and digital divide barriers for older adults
conceptual_tensions_3: Tension between multidisciplinary care ideal and healthcare system limitations in resource-constrained settings
additional_observations_1: The review uses BPS as an organizing framework rather than an explanatory model with specified mechanisms
additional_observations_2: Biological domain is most elaborated with specific aging mechanisms (sarcopenia, inflammaging, senescence)
additional_observations_3: Psychological domain is well-developed with specific constructs and interventions (CBT, ACT)
additional_observations_4: Social domain is mentioned but lacks substantive development beyond team coordination
additional_observations_5: The review proposes a stepwise clinical implementation pathway suggesting practical application
synthesis_note: This narrative review operationalizes the biopsychosocial model as an organizing framework for geriatric myofascial pain syndrome management. It elaborates biological mechanisms (sarcopenia, inflammaging, central sensitization) and psychological constructs (catastrophizing, CBT, ACT) while mentioning social factors only in terms of multidisciplinary coordination. The integration is partial, with biological and psychological domains linked through central sensitization mechanisms, but social integration remains superficial. The review proposes practical implementation pathways but acknowledges evidence gaps for innovative approaches like digital therapeutics and senolytics in geriatric populations.
coding_rationale: BPS typology 'multifactorial' because all three domains are present but social integration is minimal. Triadic integration 'partial' because bio-psych links exist but social domain is only mentioned. Domain balance 'psych-dominant' due to extensive psychological content and interventions.

bps_operationalization_summary: The paper uses the BPS model as an organizing principle to group predictors into three domains. It does not define the model formally, nor does it specify mechanisms linking domains. Social factors are treated as proxies of illness behavior rather than classical social determinants.
integration_mechanism_summary: None proposed. The paper notes associations between biological and psychological factors (e.g., pain intensity and catastrophizing) and between psychological and social proxies (e.g., healthcare-seeking and distress), but no mechanistic pathways are specified.
emergent_labels_3: transition from acute to chronic pain
conceptual_tensions_1: The paper uses BPS as an organizing principle but social domain is operationalized via proxies (healthcare-seeking, disability) rather than classical determinants
conceptual_tensions_2: Pain persistence and pain chronicity are used as overlapping terms but not clearly distinguished in analysis
conceptual_tensions_3: Biological predictors are self-reported (pain intensity) rather than objective physiological measures, creating a measurement mismatch
additional_observations_1: The paper explicitly notes that social predictors were rarely examined, which is a self-identified gap in BPS operationalization
additional_observations_2: The GRADE assessment downgraded evidence for sleep-related and occlusal factors to very low, indicating limited empirical support for those lifestyle factors
synthesis_note: This review uses the BPS model as a post-hoc organizing framework for grouping predictors but does not integrate domains. Psychological factors (catastrophizing, depression) are elaborated; biological factors are limited to self-reported pain characteristics; social factors are proxied by illness behavior. No mechanistic cross-domain pathways are proposed.
coding_rationale: Typology is pseudo_bps because all three domains are named but social is thin and no integration is present. Triadic integration is none because domains are listed in parallel. Psych-dominant balance reflects the elaborated psychological content.

bps_operationalization_summary: The paper operationalizes BPS mainly as the content and scope of PNE: education about pain origins, biopsychosocial etiology, and biological mechanisms. Acceptance is organized around patient beliefs, relevance, setting, clinician relationship, provider confidence, and role clarity. Domains are mostly listed as determinants, not modeled as interacting mechanisms.
integration_mechanism_summary: The paper specifies some pathways: trust toward clinicians reduces pain-related neural activity and can support engagement/learning; group settings provide support that may enhance motivation/adherence; PNE biological content is expected to change pain beliefs/behaviours. quality_assessment_tools_1: jbi critical appraisal tool for qualitative research
emergent_labels_9: professional culture focused on biomedical aspects of care
conceptual_tensions_1: PNE is framed as biopsychosocial, but much of the operational content is biological pain education, so social and psychological domains enter mainly as determinants of acceptance
conceptual_tensions_2: Brain-based pain explanations may reduce tissue-damage beliefs, yet the review reports they can make pain seem invented or psychological
conceptual_tensions_3: Clinicians recognize psychological factors, but the paper finds limited tools, confidence, training, and professional culture barriers to addressing them
conceptual_tensions_4: Group PNE is described as motivating and supportive, but also potentially tiring, hard to remember, and not suitable for all patients
conceptual_tensions_5: The paper calls for mechanistic work on clinician–patient relationship, but explicitly notes a lack of experimental evidence for that relationship
additional_observations_1: The review is not a direct test of BPS as a model, it is a review of determinants of PNE acceptance

additional_observations_3: Included studies were adult chronic musculoskeletal pain patients and healthcare providers from multiple countries and care levels
additional_observations_4: The review excludes pediatric, postsurgical, cancer-related, and pregnancy-related chronic pain
additional_observations_5: PNE variants include video, booklets, metaphors, in-person sessions, group sessions, individualized sessions, and multimodal PNE+
additional_observations_6: The paper relies heavily on qualitative determinants and cites experimental evidence only selectively in the discussion

citation: Kühn et al. (2026), Pain Reports
title: Acceptance of pain neuroscience education in chronic musculoskeletal pain conditions: qualitative systematic review
authors: Lukas Kühn; Eileen Wengemuth; Lara Kleist; Kyung Eun (Anna) Choi
pain_condition_detail: chronic musculoskeletal pain conditions including low back pain, osteoarthritis, neck pain, fibromyalgia, and others
context_note: International studies from England, New Zealand, Australia, United States, Netherlands, Portugal, and Lebanon
bps_function_set: background framing; explanatory framework
bps_operationalization_summary: PNE is framed as a strategy to manage biopsychosocial aspects of chronic pain, but the review focuses on barriers and facilitators to PNE acceptance rather than operationalizing the BPS model itself. The BPS label is used descriptively to frame PNE's scope.
integration_mechanism_summary: The paper proposes that psychological factors (beliefs, relationships, professional culture) influence PNE acceptance and delivery, but does not propose biological or social mechanisms linking to these psychological factors. Integration is primarily directional from psychological to social outcomes.
quality_assessment_tools_1: jbi critical appraisal tool for qualitative research
conceptual_tensions_1: Tension between PNE's biopsychosocial framing and its actual focus on biological mechanisms with limited psychological/social integration
conceptual_tensions_2: Tension between patients' biomedical beliefs and PNE's neurocentric explanation of pain
conceptual_tensions_3: Tension between group-based PNE benefits (social support) and individualized delivery needs
additional_observations_1: The review focuses on barriers and facilitators to PNE acceptance rather than operationalizing the BPS model itself
additional_observations_2: Biological content is described in detail but not integrated with psychological or social factors
additional_observations_3: Psychological constructs are well-developed with multiple outcomes documented
additional_observations_4: Social factors are mentioned but not systematically integrated with other domains
additional_observations_5: Religious/spiritual beliefs emerge as contextual factors affecting PNE acceptance
additional_observations_6: Health literacy is identified as a key determinant of PNE effectiveness
synthesis_note: This review examines barriers and facilitators to pain neuroscience education acceptance in chronic musculoskeletal pain. While PNE is framed as a biopsychosocial intervention, the review primarily focuses on psychological factors (beliefs, relationships) and mentions biological mechanisms without substantive integration. Social factors are limited to clinician-patient relationships. The BPS label is used descriptively rather than as an integrated analytical framework.
coding_rationale: BPS typology is 'multifactorial' because all three domains are present but not integrated. Psychological domain is 'elaborated' with multiple constructs and outcomes. Biological and social domains are 'mentioned' but lack integration. No triadic integration proposed.

bps_operationalization_summary: The BPS model is used as a conceptual framework to justify multimodal self-management interventions for TMD, but the review does not operationalize the model into specific variables or measures. Instead, it uses BPS language to frame the need for comprehensive treatment approaches.
integration_mechanism_summary: none proposed
conceptual_tensions_1: Tension between invoking the biopsychosocial model as a comprehensive framework while only substantively addressing biological and psychological domains, leaving the social dimension absent from the evidence synthesis
conceptual_tensions_2: Ambiguity in defining self-management therapy components - the paper notes 'there is no clearly defined distinction between the therapeutic content of self-management therapy components', creating measurement and conceptual clarity issues
additional_observations_1: The review is an umbrella review of systematic reviews, not a primary systematic review, which limits its ability to extract primary data on BPS integration
additional_observations_2: Patient education is positioned as foundational to self-management, with the paper noting it 'constitutes a basic and essential part in managing TMD' and is 'one of several evaluated therapies'
additional_observations_3: The review identifies methodological limitations in primary studies (low certainty evidence, high risk of bias) that constrain confidence in BPS-related findings
synthesis_note: This umbrella review of TMD self-management therapies uses the biopsychosocial label to frame multifactorial treatment approaches but substantively covers only biological (TMD pathology, jaw exercises) and psychological (education, CBT, behavioral therapy) domains. The social domain is entirely absent from the evidence synthesis. Psychological concepts are well-developed with multiple intervention components and outcomes, while biological content is minimal. The BPS model serves as background framing and intervention rationale rather than an operationalized framework. This exemplifies 'multifactorial' typology where all three domains are conceptually present but only two are substantively integrated.
coding_rationale: BPS typology is 'multifactorial' because biological and psychological domains are substantively covered while social is absent. Integration is 'none' for all cross-domain pairs. Psychological domain scored 'elaborated' due to multiple named constructs and intervention components. Biological scored 'mentioned' with only TMD pathology and jaw exercises named. Social domain genuinely absent despite BPS label usage.

title: Chronic pain in transgender and gender-diverse youth: a biopsychosocial perspective
authors: Gloria T. Han; Molly Basch; Diane Chen; Lonnie Zeltzer
pain_condition_detail: Chronic primary pain including headaches, widespread musculoskeletal pain, and abdominal pain, plus chronic secondary pain associated with other health conditions in transgender and gender-diverse youth.
context_note: United States, Canada, and Sweden are cited for prevalence, identity estimates, and school-based pain data; policy stressors are described as a U.S. patchwork.
bps_function_set: background framing; conclusion; explanatory framework; intervention rationale; organizing principle; policy or practice implication
bps_operationalization_summary: The review uses biopsychosocial language as an organizing and explanatory frame, structuring content around neurobiological vulnerabilities, psychosocial distress, and societal/systemic barriers. It does not operationalize BPS into measured variables; it synthesizes mechanisms and care implications.
integration_mechanism_summary: The paper proposes several pathways: minority stress and discrimination affect HPA-axis dysregulation, cortisol, inflammation, and central sensitization; anxiety/depression amplify pain sensitivity through shared neural circuits; gender dysphoria increases bodily vigilance and avoidance behaviors; gender-affirming care may reduce distress and stigma, buffering pain-exacerbating physiological and psychological processes.
bps_model_variants_3: biopsychosocial conceptualizations and models of care
conceptual_tensions_1: The review treats chronic primary and chronic secondary pain together while also noting that mechanisms and contextual challenges may differ across the two
conceptual_tensions_2: The paper emphasizes social and systemic determinants but states that evidence on many proposed mechanisms remains limited or indirect
conceptual_tensions_3: Gender-affirming care is framed as potentially protective while some practices such as chest binding, tucking, packing, and voice training are also described as capable of causing localized pain or strain
conceptual_tensions_4: The review calls for longitudinal and mechanistic research because direct chronic pain endpoints have not been studied for pubertal suppression or subsequent GAHT
conceptual_tensions_5: Intersex youth are conceptually relevant to sex characteristics and gender diversity but are explicitly outside the review's scope
additional_observations_1: The review's BPS operationalization is primarily narrative synthesis and clinical framing rather than a coded or measured BPS framework
additional_observations_2: The review cites mechanisms such as central sensitization, HPA-axis dysregulation, inflammatory processes, and shared neural circuits as cross-domain bridges
additional_observations_3: The paper includes lifestyle behaviors only as consequences of gender dysphoria-related avoidance, not as a developed lifestyle domain
additional_observations_4: Spiritual or existential content appears only within an intersectional list of systems shaping stress and resources
additional_observations_5: The paper uses the BPS label both analytically and rhetorically, especially in the conclusion where it recommends biopsychosocial care
synthesis_note: This narrative review uses biopsychosocial framing to organize chronic pain in transgender and gender-diverse youth around neurobiological vulnerabilities, psychosocial distress, and societal/systemic barriers. It proposes multiple cross-domain mechanisms, especially through minority stress, HPA-axis dysregulation, inflammation, and central sensitization, but it does not operationalize BPS into measured constructs or a formal model.
coding_rationale: All three core domains are elaborated and linked through stress physiology, pain sensitivity, and care barriers; lifestyle and spiritual content are mentioned only briefly. The typology is true_integrative because the paper relates all domains, though not with a fully specified unified mechanism.

title: Chronic pain in transgender and gender-diverse youth: a biopsychosocial perspective
authors: Gloria T. Han; Molly Basch; Diane Chen; Lonnie Zeltzer
pain_condition_detail: chronic pain in transgender and gender-diverse youth
context_note: United States and Sweden; focuses on gender-diverse youth populations
bps_function_set: background framing; conclusion; explanatory framework; organizing principle; policy or practice implication
bps_operationalization_summary: Organizes review into biological, psychological, and social/systemic sections without explicit integration mechanisms; BPS serves as explanatory framework for pain etiology in TGD youth.
integration_mechanism_summary: Psychological stressors (minority stress, gender dysphoria, discrimination) activate biological mechanisms (HPA axis dysregulation, central sensitization, hormonal influences) that amplify pain perception. Social factors like discrimination directly associate with chronic pain rates. Biological factors like estrogen and autism influence pain through neurobiological pathways.
conceptual_tensions_1: Tension between BPS integration as organizing framework and lack of specified integration mechanisms between domains
conceptual_tensions_2: Tension between acknowledging biological factors (hormones, autism) and their limited integration with psychosocial pathways
conceptual_tensions_3: Tension between advocating for gender-affirming care as solution while acknowledging lack of direct evidence for pain outcomes
additional_observations_1: Review focuses on TGD youth as a distinct population rather than applying BPS to existing chronic pain conditions
additional_observations_2: Intersectional lens applied to consider race, disability, and socioeconomic factors alongside gender identity
additional_observations_3: Double stigma concept introduced: marginalization from gender identity and from chronic pain itself
additional_observations_4: Gender-affirming care positioned as potential intervention to address both psychological distress and downstream pain effects
synthesis_note: This review applies the biopsychosocial model as an explanatory framework for chronic pain in transgender and gender-diverse youth, organizing content into biological, psychological, and social domains. While all three domains are substantively covered, integration between domains is described mechanistically only for psychosocial factors (minority stress → HPA dysregulation → central sensitization → pain). Biological factors like hormones and autism are discussed but not fully integrated with psychosocial pathways. The review identifies conceptual gaps including lack of direct measurement of pain outcomes in gender-affirming care studies and limited integration mechanisms between
coding_rationale: BPS typology as 'multifactorial' because all three domains are substantively present but integration is partial. Triadic integration as 'partial' because biological and social domains are mentioned but not integrated with each other. Psych-social integration as 'mechanistic' due to specified pathways via HPA axis and bodily vigilance.

synthesis_note: This review operationalizes the biopsychosocial model through the Theory of Pain-Sensorimotor Interactions (TOPSMI), integrating biological, psychological, and sociocultural factors through CNS plasticity mechanisms. While biological factors are well-developed, psychological and social factors are mentioned but not extensively investigated. The review demonstrates descriptive triadic integration with mechanistic elements through neuroplasticity pathways.

title: Flow-Induced Analgesia: A Conceptual Review of Biopsychosocial and Neurobiological Mechanisms of Pain Modulation
authors: Vlodeks Gromakovskis; Mārtiņš Gustavs Gūtmanis
pain_condition_detail: Chronic pain (fibromyalgia, musculoskeletal, neuropathic conditions) and acute experimental pain
bps_function_set: background framing; conclusion; explanatory framework; intervention rationale
bps_operationalization_summary: The paper uses 'biopsychosocial' as a descriptive label for pain experience and for the proposed FIA framework, but does not define the model or operationalize its domains. The BPS label appears twice: once in the introduction and once in the discussion, with no analytic follow-through.
integration_mechanism_summary: The paper proposes that flow suppresses DMN activity and activates dopaminergic reward pathways, which in turn engage descending pain modulatory systems (PAG-RVM). This is a directional bio-psych pathway. No social integration is proposed.
conceptual_tensions_1: The paper claims a biopsychosocial framework but provides no substantive social content, only minimal mentions of adherence and therapeutic alliance
conceptual_tensions_2: The paper distinguishes flow from distraction and mindfulness but acknowledges that many studies attribute analgesic effects to distraction or emotional modulation, not flow
conceptual_tensions_3: The paper proposes FIA as a distinct mechanism but notes that direct evidence linking flow and pain is sparse and correlational
additional_observations_1: The paper is a conceptual narrative review that proposes a novel framework (FIA) but does not systematically review the BPS model or its operationalization
additional_observations_2: The paper uses 'biopsychosocial' twice: once as a descriptor for pain experience and once to describe the FIA framework, but never defines or operationalizes the model
additional_observations_3: The paper's primary contribution is the proposal of flow as a testable mechanism for pain modulation, integrating attentional, motivational, and neurobiological processes
synthesis_note: This paper proposes flow-induced analgesia as a novel framework integrating attentional, motivational, and neurobiological mechanisms. It uses 'biopsychosocial' as a label but provides minimal social content, making it a pseudo-BPS paper. The main contribution is the conceptual integration of flow with pain modulation, not a systematic review of the BPS model.

citation: Gromakovskis & Gūtmanis (2025), Journal of Pain Research
title: Flow-Induced Analgesia: A Conceptual Review of Biopsychosocial and Neurobiological Mechanisms of Pain Modulation
authors: Vlodeks Gromakovskis; Mārtiņš Gustavs Gūtmanis
pain_condition_detail: Predominantly chronic and persistent pain, including fibromyalgia, musculoskeletal pain, neuropathic pain, rehabilitation cohorts, and acute experimental pain paradigms.
bps_function_set: explanatory framework; organizing principle
bps_operationalization_summary: Uses BPS as a broad label and FIA as operational mechanism: flow components -> attentional capture, DMN suppression, reward/PFC-striatal-PAG-RVM descending modulation -> analgesia; social content is mainly implementation, not social determinants.
integration_mechanism_summary: Proposed mechanisms: flow -> attentional capture/DMN suppression/reward-PFC-striatal-PAG-RVM/endogenous opioid and endocannabinoid modulation -> analgesia. Flow also -> motivation/adherence/rehabilitation outcomes. Social content is mostly implementation; no full three-domain mechanism is specified.
bps_model_variants_3: biopsychosocial and neurobiological mechanisms of pain modulation
conceptual_tensions_1: The BPS label is used, but the substantive integration is mainly psychological-neurobiological while social content is mostly clinical implementation
conceptual_tensions_2: FIA is proposed as a mechanism, yet the authors repeatedly state that evidence is correlational and causal pathways are unestablished
conceptual_tensions_3: Flow is distinguished from distraction and mindfulness, but it shares attentional and affective features with both
conceptual_tensions_4: Direct flow-pain evidence is sparse, while indirect evidence from VR, music, arts, sports, and rehabilitation is used to support the hypothesis
conceptual_tensions_5: Flow interventions are framed as beneficial, but barriers such as depression, cognitive impairment, low motivation, and excessive immersion are also named
additional_observations_1: Formal quality or bias assessment was not performed, consistent with the conceptual narrative design
additional_observations_2: The review is not a meta-analysis, approximately 40 conceptually relevant studies were qualitatively synthesized
additional_observations_3: Pain conditions are broad and include fibromyalgia, musculoskeletal pain, neuropathic pain, rehabilitation cohorts, and acute experimental pain paradigms
additional_observations_4: The biopsychosocial model is invoked but not formally defined
additional_observations_5: Operationalization occurs mainly through proposed future flow measures rather than measured constructs across all BPS domains
additional_observations_6: Social content centers on access, training, clinics, adherence, and therapeutic alliance rather than socioeconomic, cultural, or structural determinants
synthesis_note: This review uses BPS mainly as a framing label while operationalizing FIA as a psychological-neurobiological pathway. Social content is mostly implementation and access, not social determinants. It offers mechanistic bio-psych links and partial psych-social/bio-social links, but not a true triadic model.
coding_rationale: Dyadic bio-psych focus; social domain is named but thin. FIA proposes mechanisms, yet causal evidence and triadic integration remain limited.

title: Is resistance training with external loads superior to unloaded exercise in the management of chronic low back pain? A systematic review and meta-analysis
authors: Marco Ranzani; Andrea Pozzi; Daniele Fornasari; Diego Ristori; Marco Testa
pain_condition_detail: chronic non-specific low back pain
bps_function_set: background framing; conclusion; explanatory framework; intervention rationale; organizing principle
bps_operationalization_summary: The BPS model is cited as best practice for chronic NS-LBP management but is not formally defined. It serves as background framing and organizing principle for recommending individualized exercise prescription, with load effectiveness positioned within broader psychological and contextual factors rather than as a standalone mechanical intervention.
integration_mechanism_summary: The paper proposes that external load may act as a graded exposure stimulus to reduce fear-avoidance, kinesiophobia, and pain catastrophizing. However, it argues that improvements in pain and disability are not determined by tissue adaptation alone but rather by psychological and contextual factors, suggesting load effectiveness depends on integration within a broader biopsychosocial framework.
conceptual_tensions_1: Tension between BPS label usage and actual domain coverage: the model is invoked as best practice but the social domain is entirely absent from the analysis
conceptual_tensions_2: Tension between proposed psychological mechanisms (graded exposure, behavioral re-signification) and actual measurement: key constructs like kinesiophobia are not measured, and pain catastrophizing only in one study
conceptual_tensions_3: Tension between clinical recommendation for individualized, BPS-informed exercise and the evidence base showing load effects are comparable to unloaded exercise
additional_observations_1: The review demonstrates that BPS language is used extensively but the social domain is completely absent from the substantive analysis, representing a significant gap in the model's operationalization
additional_observations_2: Psychological constructs are theorized as mechanisms (fear-avoidance, catastrophizing) but empirical measurement is inadequate, with kinesiophobia unmeasured and pain catastrophizing only in one study
additional_observations_3: The paper proposes that load effectiveness depends on contextual factors (therapeutic framing, patient interpretation) rather than mechanical properties alone, positioning load as a behavioral signal rather than a treatment component
synthesis_note: This review operationalizes the BPS model primarily through biological and psychological constructs, with the social domain entirely absent. While the BPS label is used extensively as background framing and for recommending individualized care, the actual integration across domains is limited to a directional bio-psychological relationship (load → fear-avoidance). The paper reveals a gap between BPS rhetoric and substantive three-domain integration, with psychological constructs underreported empirically despite theoretical importance.
coding_rationale: BPS typology is 'multifactorial' because biological and psychological domains are substantively present but social domain is absent. Triadic integration is 'none' due to complete absence of social factors. Bio-psych integration is 'directional' based on theorized graded exposure mechanism.

bps_function_set: background framing; conclusion; organizing principle
bps_operationalization_summary: The paper uses the biopsychosocial label as an organizing principle to situate fascia within a multifactorial framework, but never defines the model. integration_mechanism_summary: The paper proposes that fascial pathology generates nociceptive input leading to central sensitization (bio-psych directional). additional_observations_2: The paper uses the term 'biopsychosocial' as an organizing principle but never defines what the model means, and the social domain is limited to a single factor ('inactivity')
synthesis_note: This narrative review elaborates biological mechanisms of fascial pathology in myofascial pain syndrome but uses the biopsychosocial label as an organizing principle without defining the model. Psychological factors are named but not defined, and social content is minimal. Integration is partial: biological and psychological domains are directionally linked via central sensitization, but no three-domain mechanism is proposed.
coding_rationale: Typology is pseudo_bps because BPS language is used but social domain is minimal and psychological constructs are only named. pain_condition_detail: Myofascial pain syndrome (MPS), described as localized or regional pain with taut bands and myofascial trigger points reproducing referred pain when palpated.
context_note: Paper references the general population, specialized pain clinics, chronic low back and neck pain, and international initiatives for consensus terminology.
bps_function_set: explanatory framework; intervention rationale; operational definition; organizing principle; policy or practice implication
bps_operationalization_summary: The paper uses BPS mainly as an organizing and explanatory frame for a fascia-centered MPS model. It lists fascia, muscle, neural, and psychosocial factors, then links some through peripheral input, central sensitization, neuroimmune pathways, and multimodal treatment. It does not provide formal BPS definitions or operationalized variables.
integration_mechanism_summary: The main mechanism is peripheral-to-central: fascial densification, fibrosis, and inflammation generate nociceptive input, which contributes to peripheral sensitization, central sensitization, dorsal horn hyperexcitability, descending control changes, and cortical reorganization. Psychosocial factors are said to amplify pain through neuroimmune and central pathways, but no detailed psychosocial mechanism is specified.
quality_assessment_tools_1: sanra (scale for the assessment of narrative review articles)
conceptual_tensions_1: The paper argues for fascia as a central peripheral driver while also insisting that fascia should not be viewed in isolation
conceptual_tensions_2: It uses a biopsychosocial frame but gives much more substantive attention to fascia and central sensitization than to social factors
conceptual_tensions_3: It proposes psychosocial factors amplify pain through neuroimmune and central pathways but does not elaborate the psychosocial mechanism
conceptual_tensions_4: It criticizes muscle-centric and central sensitization models as incomplete, while proposing fascia as a unifying substrate that may risk reductionism if psychosocial domains are ignored
additional_observations_1: The article is a conceptual narrative review, not a systematic review or meta-analysis, despite searching PubMed, Embase, Scopus, and Google Scholar
additional_observations_2: The review's most concrete operationalization is a named integrative conceptual model with fascial pathology, muscular dysfunction, central sensitization, and psychosocial influences
additional_observations_3: Psychological and social constructs are named but not measured, defined, or linked to specific instruments
additional_observations_4: The social domain is essentially collapsed into psychosocial factors, with no named social determinants such as work, family, healthcare access, or socioeconomic position
synthesis_note: This review operationalizes BPS as a fascia-centered explanatory frame for MPS. Biological content is rich and sustained, especially fascia, nociception, inflammation, mechanotransduction, and central sensitization. Psychological content is present but mostly listed and undifferentiated. Social content is thin and underexplored. The paper proposes peripheral-to-central and neuroimmune pathways, but triadic integration remains partial rather than a fully specified three-domain mechanism.
coding_rationale: Bio-dominant pseudo-BPS: BPS is used analytically to organize fascia, muscle, neural, and psychosocial content, but social factors are minimally specified and triadic integration is mostly parallel with some peripheral-to-central mechanisms.

title: Exploring fascia in myofascial pain syndrome: an integrative model of mechanisms
authors: Vlodeks Gromakovskis

bps_function_set: background framing; conclusion; explanatory framework; organizing principle; policy or practice implication
bps_operationalization_summary: The paper operationalizes BPS by integrating fascial pathology with muscle dysfunction, central sensitization, and psychosocial factors into a conceptual model that explains MPS heterogeneity and guides multimodal treatment.
integration_mechanism_summary: The paper proposes that fascial pathology generates nociceptive input that drives central sensitization, while psychological stress amplifies pain through neuroimmune pathways. All three domains form a descriptive integrative model without specified mechanistic pathways.
conceptual_tensions_1: Tension between fascia-focused biological model and incomplete integration of psychosocial domain
conceptual_tensions_2: Tension between historical muscle-centric models and emerging fascial mechanisms
conceptual_tensions_3: Tension between descriptive triadic integration and lack of specified mechanistic pathways
additional_observations_1: The paper uses BPS terminology extensively but primarily develops the biological domain with fascial mechanisms
additional_observations_2: Psychological and social factors are mentioned but not elaborated with specific constructs or measures
additional_observations_3: The integrative model is presented descriptively rather than through specified mechanistic pathways
additional_observations_4: The paper acknowledges its own limitations in psychosocial domain coverage
synthesis_note: This paper operationalizes the biopsychosocial model by integrating fascial pathology with muscle dysfunction, central sensitization, and psychosocial factors into a conceptual model for MPS. While the biological domain is elaborately developed with fascial mechanisms, psychological and social domains are minimally covered. The integration is descriptive rather than mechanistic, with fascial pathology positioned as a peripheral driver that interacts with central and psychosocial factors. The paper acknowledges gaps in psychosocial integration and terminology standardization.
coding_rationale: BPS typology is multifactorial because all three domains are present but biological domain is elaborated while others are mentioned. Triadic integration is descriptive because all domains are related but no mechanistic pathways are specified. Biological coverage is elaborated due to detailed fascial mechanisms; psychological and social are mentioned due to brief references to stress and inactivity.

title: Social factors contributing to the development of chronic low back pain: a scoping review
authors: Yvan Sonjon; Annabelle Gonthier; Camille Lépingle; Jean-Baptiste Van der Henst; Karen T. Reilly; Eric Chabanat
pain_condition_detail: non-specific chronic low back pain (CLBP), defined as pain in the lumbar region present for at least 3 months
context_note: Focused on industrialized Western countries; includes primary, secondary, and tertiary care settings.
bps_function_set: background framing; conclusion; justification; organizing principle
bps_operationalization_summary: The paper uses the BPS model as an organizing principle to scope social factors in CLBP. It defines social factors broadly as external influences, reclassifies some biological/psychological factors as socially shaped, and proposes a six-domain classification. No cross-domain mechanisms are specified; integration is absent.
integration_mechanism_summary: None proposed. The paper describes associations between social factors and psychological constructs (e.g., depression mediating social status and pain, stress mediating income and pain) but specifies no pathways or processes.
emergent_labels_4: MacArthur Scale of Subjective Social Status
conceptual_tensions_1: Paper reclassifies biological/psychological factors as social (e.g., BMI, sleep) but does not specify mechanisms linking them to social determinants
conceptual_tensions_2: Claims BPS model involves 'complex interactions' but only lists social factors in parallel, no cross-domain integration is provided
conceptual_tensions_3: Acknowledges boundary issues between BPS domains but does not resolve them, uses broad definition of social factors that may dilute specificity
additional_observations_1: The paper is a scoping review that explicitly focuses on social factors, with minimal biological and psychological content. It uses BPS as an organizing principle to justify its scope but does not integrate domains
additional_observations_2: The classification system (six domains) is the main contribution, it is descriptive and does not propose causal pathways
additional_observations_3: The paper critiques the literature for treating social factors as adjustment variables rather than explanatory ones, but does not itself model them as such
synthesis_note: This scoping review provides a comprehensive classification of social factors in CLBP (28 categories, 6 domains) but does not integrate biological, psychological, and social domains. BPS is used as an organizing principle; no mechanisms or pathways are specified. The paper is social-dominant with minimal biological and psychological coverage, illustrating a common pattern of BPS language without substantive integration.
coding_rationale: Typology 'pseudo_bps' because BPS language is used but biological and psychological domains are thin. Triadic integration is 'none' as domains are listed in parallel. Social domain is elaborated; biological and psychological are minimal/mentioned.

pain_condition_detail: Adult non-specific chronic low back pain (CLBP), defined as lumbar pain for at least 3 months after acute causes/treatments have been addressed.
context_note: Industrialized Western countries with comparable relational, cultural, political frameworks and healthcare structures/delivery models; WEIRD limitation noted.

integration_mechanism_summary: No three-domain mechanism proposed. It proposes social determinants shaping lifestyle/health indicators and stigma affecting care access, and psychosocial mediators such as depression and perceived stress linking social conditions to pain outcomes; biological, psychological, and social factors are not modeled as a single system.

emergent_labels_12: health literacy specific to low back pain

conceptual_tensions_2: Biological or psychological factors are reclassified as social when socially shaped, creating a debatable boundary between domains
conceptual_tensions_3: Social relationships are described as important for recovery, yet family and professional support remain underexplored
conceptual_tensions_4: Social factors are often treated as adjustment variables or economic impacts rather than explanatory contributors to CLBP progression
conceptual_tensions_5: Western WEIRD restriction may underrepresent marginalized populations and systemic or cultural injustice
additional_observations_1: The review explicitly states that included studies used a BPS model, but its own synthesis is a descriptive classification of social factors
additional_observations_2: No critical appraisal or risk-of-bias assessment was conducted because the authors judged it inappropriate for the scoping-review aim
additional_observations_3: The review says its reclassification of biological or psychological factors as social is descriptive and does not reinterpret original findings
additional_observations_4: The paper recommends mixed methods and participatory action research for underrepresented domains
additional_observations_5: The review calls for hypothesis-driven research to test temporal and potentially causal links between social factors and CLBP evolution
synthesis_note: This review operationalizes BPS mainly as a social lens for CLBP. It elaborates social and psychosocial factors, mentions biological/lifestyle factors when socially shaped, and uses BPS to justify classification and care strategies. It names pairwise pathways, especially social-psychological mediators, but does not model a three-domain system.
coding_rationale: Social-dominant pseudo-BPS: BPS organizes the review and care rationale, but biological content is thin and triadic integration is absent.

bps_operationalization_summary: Organizes the review into six social domains (socio-demographic, socio-occupational, socio-environmental, global health data, psycho-social, patient experience of healthcare) and categorizes 28 factor types, treating biological and psychological factors as socially shaped rather than maintaining distinct domains.
integration_mechanism_summary: Three directional claims: depression mediates social status to pain severity; perceived stress mediates household income to pain persistence; social support influences self-efficacy affecting CLBP outcomes. No biological domain integration proposed.
conceptual_tensions_1: Tension between BPS theoretical framework and practical treatment of biological and psychological factors as socially shaped
conceptual_tensions_2: Gap between BPS label usage and actual integration of three domains in CLBP research
conceptual_tensions_3: Underrepresentation of interpersonal and family-level social factors despite their recognized importance
additional_observations_1: Review focuses exclusively on social factors, treating biological and psychological factors as socially determined rather than maintaining distinct domains
additional_observations_2: Classification system organizes 28 factor categories into 6 social domains, with Global Health Data domain including traditionally biological factors (BMI, sleep) re-conceptualized as social
additional_observations_3: No formal quality appraisal conducted, consistent with scoping review methodology but limits ability to assess strength of evidence
additional_observations_4: Citation network analysis reveals fragmented literature with limited cross-citation between studies
synthesis_note: This scoping review operationalizes the BPS model by organizing social factors into six domains and 28 categories, treating biological and psychological factors as socially shaped. It identifies significant gaps in social factor research, particularly for interpersonal relationships, and critiques current clinical assessment tools for inadequately capturing social dimensions. The review demonstrates how BPS language can serve as an organizing principle while substantive three-domain integration remains absent.
coding_rationale: Scored social domain as elaborated due to 28 factor categories organized into 6 domains; psychological as mentioned due to 9 named constructs; biological as absent. Triadic integration scored as none due to absence of biological domain. BPS typology as multifactorial because all three domains present but social dominates. Integration claims identified 3 directional relationships between psychological and social factors.

title: Social dimensions as explanatory approaches for the development of chronic pain: a meta-ethnography of qualitative studies
authors: Sarah Potthoff; Dominik Koesling; Claudia Bozzaro
journal: International Journal for Equity in Health
fulltext_exclusion_reason: fewer than two domains substantively covered
pain_condition_detail: chronic non-malignant pain, especially low back pain and headache disorders, also fibromyalgia, complex regional pain syndrome, non-specific chronic low back pain
context_note: Studies from Canada, USA, UK, Australia, Norway, Sweden, Spain, Germany, Chile, Ethiopia, Switzerland, Jordan, worldwide online; focus on marginalized groups.
bps_function_set: background framing; conclusion; critique or problematization
bps_operationalization_summary: The paper uses BPS as background framing to justify focusing on the neglected social dimension. It does not operationalize BPS itself; instead, it critiques the model for lacking theoretical foundations in social analysis and conducts a meta-ethnography exclusively on social dimensions, leaving biomedical and psychological aspects unanalyzed.
integration_mechanism_summary: None proposed. The paper describes associations between social factors (e.g., stigmatization, adversities, high expectations, loneliness) and chronic pain, but does not specify pathways or mechanisms linking social to psychological or biological domains.
quality_assessment_tools_1: jbi critical appraisal checklist for qualitative research
emergent_labels_2: stigmatization, discrimination, and marginalization based on social identity
emergent_labels_5: high expectations regarding work or school
emergent_labels_6: cultural and religious beliefs and values
conceptual_tensions_1: Paper critiques BPS for neglecting social dimension, but its own analysis also neglects biological and psychological domains, reproducing the same imbalance in reverse
conceptual_tensions_2: Lifestyle factors are categorized as a social dimension, but could also be considered individual behavioral or psychological factors, creating ambiguity
conceptual_tensions_3: The paper excludes studies that treat social as 'individual psychosocial phenomenon from a psychological perspective', yet some included social factors (e.g., stoicism, loneliness) have strong psychological components
additional_observations_1: The paper is a meta-ethnography of qualitative studies, not a systematic review of quantitative evidence, its contribution is conceptual and interpretive
additional_observations_2: The paper explicitly states it did not analyze additional study results beyond those related to social dimensions, meaning it deliberately excluded biological and psychological content from included studies
additional_observations_3: The paper uses BPS as a rhetorical foil to justify a single-domain (social) analysis, rather than operationalizing BPS as an integrative framework
synthesis_note: This meta-ethnography contributes a rich taxonomy of eight social dimensions (gender inequity, stigmatization, adversities, harsh conditions, high expectations, cultural beliefs, loneliness, lifestyle) as explanatory factors for chronic pain. However, it does not operationalize the biopsychosocial model integratively: biological and psychological domains are minimally present, and no cross-domain mechanisms are proposed. The paper critiques BPS for neglecting the social but reproduces the same imbalance by focusing exclusively on social factors.
coding_rationale: Typology is pseudo_bps because BPS language is used but only the social domain is elaborated; biology and psychology are minimal. Triadic integration is none because domains are not related. Social-dominant balance reflects the paper's exclusive focus on social dimensions.

title: Social dimensions as explanatory approaches for the development of chronic pain: a meta-ethnography of qualitative studies
authors: Sarah Potthoff; Dominik Koesling; Claudia Bozzaro
journal: International Journal for Equity in Health
pain_condition_detail: Chronic non-malignant pain, especially chronic low back pain and headache disorders.
context_note: Worldwide studies; most in Anglo-American countries, with migration, refugee history, and disadvantaged neighborhoods as recurring contexts.

bps_operationalization_summary: The paper uses BPS mainly as a critique: it names biomedical, psychological, and social etiologies but operationalizes the review by excluding psychosocial-only studies and synthesizing social dimensions. Biological and psychological content appear as background/context, not integrated mechanisms.
integration_mechanism_summary: Social-to-psychological mechanisms dominate: stigma and gendered expectations can delay care, high expectations create stress and insufficient recovery, cultural stoicism delays treatment, and collectivist priorities reduce adherence. Trauma is framed as triggering pain and mental health consequences; biomedical content is mostly background.

conceptual_tensions_3: Quantitative social-factor studies are said to be limited because they focus on objective, measurable factors rather than subtle interactions and patient experience
conceptual_tensions_4: Gender is treated both as biological sex and as gender relations/social inequality, and the review privileges the latter
conceptual_tensions_5: The review excludes studies that discuss the social merely as an individual psychosocial phenomenon, so psychological material appears but is not analyzed as a psychological domain
additional_observations_1: The review’s inclusion criteria explicitly excluded studies that discussed the social merely as an individual psychosocial phenomenon from a psychological perspective

additional_observations_3: Included studies were worldwide but concentrated in Anglo-American countries, English and German language limits are named as limitations

additional_observations_5: The paper treats lifestyle factors as an eighth social dimension rather than as a separate lifestyle framework

title: Social dimensions as explanatory approaches for the development of chronic pain: a meta-ethnography of qualitative studies
authors: Sarah Potthoff; Dominik Koesling; Claudia Bozzaro
journal: International Journal for Equity in Health
fulltext_exclusion_reason: single-domain review with no cross-domain claim
pain_condition_detail: chronic pain, especially low back pain and headache disorders
context_note: Global review with studies from Canada, USA, UK, Australia, Europe, Africa, Asia, and worldwide online
bps_function_set: background framing; organizing principle; policy or practice implication
bps_operationalization_summary: Uses BPS as organizing framework to structure review of social dimensions, but focuses exclusively on social factors through meta-ethnography of qualitative studies, treating biological and psychological as secondary contexts.
integration_mechanism_summary: none proposed
quality_assessment_tools_1: jbi critical appraisal checklist for qualitative research
conceptual_tensions_1: Tension between BPS label usage and actual social-only focus - the review uses BPS terminology but conducts meta-ethnography exclusively on social dimensions
conceptual_tensions_2: Tension between quantitative recognition of social factors (gender, SES, discrimination) and qualitative exploration of subtle societal interactions like recognition/exclusion
conceptual_tensions_3: Tension between individual psychosocial framing and sociological perspective - social is equated with subjective/individual and subsumed under psychological
additional_observations_1: This is a meta-ethnography that synthesizes qualitative studies to generate theoretical knowledge about social dimensions, using Noblit and Hare's methodological framework
additional_observations_2: The review explicitly excludes studies that discuss social merely as individual psychosocial phenomenon from psychological perspective, maintaining sociological focus
additional_observations_3: Eight social dimensions identified as third-order constructs from 27 included qualitative studies across 1997-2024
additional_observations_4: Strong emphasis on intersectionality - how multiple social dimensions (gender, migration status, ethnicity) interact to influence pain chronicity
additional_observations_5: Policy implications extend beyond healthcare to include housing, employment, childcare, and anti-discrimination programs
synthesis_note: This meta-ethnography exclusively focuses on social dimensions of chronic pain through qualitative synthesis, using BPS as an organizing framework but not integrating biological or psychological domains. It identifies eight social dimensions and critiques the BPS literature for neglecting social factors. The review's contribution is mapping social explanatory approaches through meta-ethnography rather than testing BPS integration.
coding_rationale: BPS typology is 'narrow_despite_label' because the review uses BPS terminology but focuses exclusively on social dimensions through meta-ethnography. Triadic integration is 'none' because biological and psychological domains are absent from substantive analysis. Social domain is 'elaborated' with eight named dimensions.

The review focuses on OMT effectiveness and healthcare access barriers rather than BPS operationalization. Pain conditions studied include chronic low back pain and musculoskeletal pain in rural/underserved populations across multiple countries.
coding_rationale: BPS typology is 'multifactorial' because all three domains are mentioned but not integrated. Triadic integration is 'none' because domains are listed in parallel without specified relationships. Concept definitions are 'partial' because some constructs like fear avoidance are described informally while others like depression are only named.

citation: Rinaudo et al. (2025), PLOS One
title: Navigating the biopsychosocial landscape: A systematic review on the association between social support and chronic pain
authors: Carlo Matej Rinaudo; Maxim Van de Velde; Arnaud Steyaert; André Mouraux; Bianka Karshikoff
pain_condition_detail: Chronic pain (persistent or recurrent pain lasting longer than 3 months), including musculoskeletal pain, fibromyalgia, spinal cord injury, neurological/neuromuscular pain or disability, chronic migraine/headache, post-surgical pain, chronic pelvic pain, articular pain, and unspecified chronic pain.
context_note: Studies were mainly conducted in the USA, Canada or Europe; only three studies were outside these regions (South Korea and Australia); authors note Western-country generalisability limits.
bps_function_set: background framing; explanatory framework; justification
bps_operationalization_summary: The review uses BPS mainly to justify a social-support focus, then operationalizes only social support (PSS, SSS, SpR) and compares them with pain, QoL, depression, and anxiety outcomes. It does not code or model biological, psychological, and social domains as an integrated system.
integration_mechanism_summary: The paper proposes a social-support pathway in which support buffers stress through stress appraisal and active coping, potentially reducing pain; spousal responses may reinforce pain behaviour through operant learning. It does not specify a full three-domain mechanism in which biological, psychological, and social factors reciprocally shape one another.
quality_assessment_tools_1: adapted version of the “jbi critical appraisal checklist for analytical cross-sectional studies”
quality_assessment_tools_3: adapted version of the quality assessment tool of hawker et al
emergent_labels_11: operant conditioning theory of chronic pain
conceptual_tensions_1: The BPS label frames chronic pain as biological, psychological, and social, but the review’s operational exposure is social support rather than all three domains
conceptual_tensions_2: Social support generally appears beneficial, but spousal responses can be associated with worse pain, disability, and depression
conceptual_tensions_3: The evidence base is mostly cross-sectional and correlational, yet the paper discusses possible causality and future longitudinal designs
conceptual_tensions_4: Different social support constructs and questionnaires create inconsistency and obscure whether PSS, SSS, and SpR have comparable meanings
conceptual_tensions_5: Spousal responses are explicitly not a measure of social support per se, yet they are included as an important chronic-pain social factor
additional_observations_1: The review does not perform meta-analysis, it uses vote counting and correlation/regression direction because of heterogeneity and lack of effect sizes
additional_observations_2: No included studies were randomized, and only eight of 40 final studies were longitudinal
additional_observations_3: Spousal responses are treated as a social exposure because they influence pain behaviour and well-being, even though the paper says they are not social support per se
additional_observations_4: The paper’s closest triadic mechanism is stress-buffering through stress appraisal and active coping, but it is not tied to a full BPS operational model
additional_observations_5: Biological content is concentrated in pain/nociception definitions and pain outcomes rather than mechanisms such as inflammation, genetics, imaging, or peripheral sensitization
additional_observations_6: The conclusion recommends spouse education and including spouses in treatment sessions, which turns social support findings into applied pain-management suggestions
synthesis_note: This review uses a BPS-labeled title/intro but operationalizes social support rather than the full BPS model. It codes PSS, SSS, and SpR against pain, QoL, depression, and anxiety, mostly with cross-sectional correlations. It offers stress-buffering and operant-learning pathways but no full biological-psychological-social system.
coding_rationale: Social support dominates; psychological outcomes are developed; biological content is limited to pain/nociception. BPS frames the topic but does not create a triadic mechanism, so pseudo_bps/partial integration.

citation: Tjell et al. (2025), Frontiers in Neurology
title: Poly-symptomatology of chronic multi-canalicular benign paroxysmal positional vertigo: a deductive, inductive, and abductive narrative review
authors: Carsten Tjell; Wenche Iglebekk; Peter Borenstein
pain_condition_detail: chronic multi-canalicular benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (mc-BPPV)
bps_function_set: background framing; organizing principle
bps_operationalization_summary: The BPS label is used to frame the diagnostic challenge of mc-BPPV when objective findings are absent, positioning it as an alternative to psychological disorder diagnosis rather than an integrative framework.
integration_mechanism_summary: The paper proposes that vestibular abnormalities in mc-BPPV cause downstream symptoms through specific neural pathways: vestibulo-thalamo-cortical activity leads to cognitive dysfunction, trigeminal activation causes TMJ pain, non-classical auditory pathways produce tinnitus, and vestibulo-thalamo-hypothalamic activity contributes to fatigue.
pain_conditions_1: chronic multi-canalicular benign paroxysmal positional vertigo
conceptual_tensions_1: Tension between BPS diagnostic framing and complete absence of social domain content
conceptual_tensions_2: BPS label used to position mc-BPPV as alternative to psychological disorder, but no actual psychological constructs integrated
additional_observations_1: The review uses a tripartite classification (deductive, inductive, abductive) to grade symptom relationships to mc-BPPV
additional_observations_2: Symptoms are categorized by strength of evidence rather than theoretical integration
additional_observations_3: The paper explicitly questions whether anterior SCC involvement can be iatrogenic from Brandt-Daroff exercises
synthesis_note: This review uses the BPS label to frame mc-BPPV as a diagnostic consideration when objective findings are absent, but provides no social domain content. Biological mechanisms are well-developed, showing how vestibular dysfunction causes downstream symptoms via specific neural pathways. Psychological content is minimal, limited to cognitive symptoms linked to vestibular-thalamo-cortical activity. The BPS label functions as background framing rather than an integrative framework.
coding_rationale: BPS typology is multifactorial due to elaborated biological content and minimal psychological content with no social domain. Integration is directional bio-psych via specific neural pathways, not mechanistic triadic integration. BPS label serves as diagnostic framing, not analytical framework.

integration_mechanism_summary: None proposed. The paper asserts that stress leads to stronger pain responses and that social support reduces stress and pain, but no pathway or mediator is specified. Biological, psychological, and social factors are discussed separately without triadic integration.
conceptual_tensions_1: The paper advocates for integrative lifestyle medicine but presents it as a separate approach from interventional pain management, not as an integrated model
conceptual_tensions_2: Biopsychosocial model is invoked only as background framing, the paper's actual framework is lifestyle medicine with six parallel pillars
conceptual_tensions_3: Psychological constructs (stress, anxiety, emotional processing) are mentioned but never defined or measured, the paper relies on biological mechanisms for most claims
additional_observations_1: The paper is a debate-style narrative review, not a systematic review, it presents two opposing viewpoints (integrative vs. interventional) without synthesizing evidence
additional_observations_2: Lifestyle medicine is treated as the operationalization of the biopsychosocial model, but the six pillars are listed in parallel without cross-domain integration
additional_observations_3: Telemedicine is proposed as a solution to barriers of lifestyle medicine (time, cost, adherence) but is not linked to the biopsychosocial model
synthesis_note: This paper uses the biopsychosocial label only as background framing and does not operationalize the model. It elaborates biological mechanisms (inflammation, obesity, sleep) and lifestyle factors but treats psychological and social domains superficially. No triadic integration is present; the paper is a debate on lifestyle medicine vs. interventional approaches.
coding_rationale: Typology is pseudo_bps because BPS label appears but psychological and social domains are thin. Triadic integration is none because domains are discussed separately. Close call on bio coverage: elaborated due to detailed inflammatory and metabolic mechanisms.

title: A debate on integrative vs . interventional approaches to chronic pain: does telemedicine play a role?
authors: Kush Patel; Leena Mathew; Alopi Patel
pain_condition_detail: Chronic pain in general, with examples including spinal pain, osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, chronic lower back pain, fibromyalgia, migraines, and neurodegenerative disease.
context_note: Discusses Western medicine, insurance coverage, rural access, socioeconomic inequities, and access to healthy foods or safe exercise environments.
bps_function_set: background framing; intervention rationale; organizing principle; policy or practice implication
bps_operationalization_summary: The paper uses the BPS label to frame chronic pain as biological, psychological, and socio-environmental, but operationalizes the argument mainly through lifestyle medicine pillars, telemedicine access, and barriers to implementation rather than measuring or modeling domain interactions.
integration_mechanism_summary: The paper proposes biological and psychological mechanisms for nutrition, stress, sleep, substances, and exercise, and social mechanisms for support, access, and healthcare systems. It does not specify a full three-domain pathway in which biological, psychological, and social factors act on one another as a single system.
conceptual_tensions_1: The article frames pain as biopsychosocial but operationalizes most of the argument through lifestyle medicine, telemedicine access, and reimbursement barriers
conceptual_tensions_2: Integrative care is presented as comprehensive, while interventional pain medicine is justified by anatomical and neurochemical pathways and rapid analgesia
conceptual_tensions_3: Lifestyle medicine is described as evidence-based and beneficial, but constrained by time, training, adherence, resources, and insurance coverage
conceptual_tensions_4: Telemedicine is presented as a solution to time and access barriers but itself has technical, physical-exam, tool-access, and security limitations
conceptual_tensions_5: The paper names future outcome measures but does not specify instruments or validated measures for the constructs it discusses
additional_observations_1: The article is a debate rather than a systematic review or empirical study, so no quality assessment or risk-of-bias tools are reported
additional_observations_2: The paper’s strongest integration is within the biological-psychological interface, especially stress, sleep, inflammation, and substance use
additional_observations_3: Social content is substantial but mainly concerns access, support, insurance, reimbursement, policy, and telemedicine, not interpersonal mechanisms in pain care
additional_observations_4: The paper treats telemedicine as an implementation infrastructure rather than as a psychological, biological, or social construct
synthesis_note: This paper uses the biopsychosocial label to justify lifestyle medicine for chronic pain, but its substantive content is dominated by lifestyle, biomedical, and healthcare-system factors. Psychological content appears mainly as stress, anxiety, fatigue, mental health, adherence, and behavioral change. It offers some biological-psychological and social-psychological pathways, but not a full three-domain mechanism.
coding_rationale: BPS is explicit but mostly organizational. Lifestyle medicine supplies the operational content, with elaborated biological, lifestyle, and social domains, mentioned psychological content, and partial triadic integration.

conceptual_tensions_1: The review invokes a comprehensive BPS model but does not define it or use it to select, measure, or model variables
conceptual_tensions_2: Prevalence heterogeneity is attributed to diagnostic criteria, cutoffs, and assessment tools, yet these sources of variation are not modeled
conceptual_tensions_3: Narrative associations between sociodemographic features and CP are not statistically significant in meta-regression

synthesis_note: This review operationalizes BPS only as a rationale for comprehensive, multimodal care after a prevalence-focused synthesis. authors: Katrina S. Monroe; Kristin R. Archer; Stephen T. Wegener; Sara P. Gombatto

bps_function_set: background framing; critique or problematization; intervention rationale; justification; organizing principle
bps_operationalization_summary: The paper uses BPS as a foundation for PIPT but focuses on bio (exercise, physical activity) and psycho (cognitive skill training) domains, explicitly noting that social factors are rarely addressed.
