integration_mechanism_summary: The model proposes that PIPT interventions (cognitive skill training + exercise) reduce pain-related disability through psychological mediators (psychological flexibility, self-efficacy, reduced catastrophizing/fear avoidance) and physical mediators (improved movement patterns). Social factors are contextual moderators but not integrated into the causal pathway.
conceptual_tensions_1: The paper uses BPS as a foundation but explicitly notes that social factors are rarely addressed in BPS-labeled PT, creating a tension between the model's claim and its operationalization
conceptual_tensions_2: The logic model integrates bio and psych domains via mediators but treats social factors as contextual moderators rather than integrated components, reflecting a partial triadic integration
conceptual_tensions_3: Psychological constructs like catastrophizing and fear avoidance are named but not formally defined, relying on assumed shared meaning
additional_observations_1: The paper proposes a logic model for PIPT that is explicitly designed to be culturally tailored, but the general model itself does not include social factors as essential intervention components
additional_observations_2: The paper's literature review on Latino populations provides rich social and cultural detail, but this is not integrated into the causal pathway of the logic model
additional_observations_3: The paper critiques existing BPS frameworks for lacking specificity and sociocultural consideration, yet its own model does not fully operationalize the social domain
synthesis_note: This paper uses BPS as a foundation for PIPT but operationalizes it primarily as bio+psych, with social factors acknowledged but not integrated into the causal model. It explicitly critiques BPS-labeled PT for neglecting social factors, yet its own logic model does not fully address this gap. The paper is valuable for its focus on cultural tailoring and its explicit identification of conceptual problems with BPS.
coding_rationale: Typology is pseudo_bps because BPS language is used but social domain is thin and not integrated. Triadic integration is partial: bio and psych are linked via mediators, social is contextual. Psych-dominant due to elaborated psychological constructs.

citation: Monroe et al. (2025), The journal of pain
title: Psychologically Informed Physical Therapy Management of Chronic Musculoskeletal Pain in Culturally Diverse Populations: An Intervention Logic Model
authors: Katrina S. Monroe; Kristin R. Archer; Stephen T. Wegener; Sara P. Gombatto
pain_condition_detail: Chronic musculoskeletal pain; examples include low back pain, neck pain, and chronic spine pain.
context_note: Illustration focuses on US Hispanic/Latino persons seeking care for chronic spine pain at a Federally Qualified Health Center near the United States-Mexico border; broader context includes CALD populations and low- and middle-income nations.
bps_function_set: background framing; critique or problematization; intervention rationale; justification; operational definition; organizing principle; policy or practice implication
bps_operationalization_summary: The paper turns the BPS frame into a PIPT logic model: cognitive skill training plus aerobic activity, therapeutic exercise, and graded functional movement. It specifies determinants such as psychological flexibility, self-efficacy, catastrophizing, fear, and pain beliefs, and tailors them to sociocultural factors such as language, health literacy, familismo, personalismo, and social support.
integration_mechanism_summary: PIPT combines cognitive skill training with aerobic activity, therapeutic exercise, and graded functional movement. The proposed pathway is active cognitive and physical coping behaviors, mediated by psychological flexibility, self-efficacy, reduced catastrophizing/fear/maladaptive beliefs, leading to less pain/disability and greater work/social participation. Sociocultural factors are proposed as moderators/mediators and tailoring guides, not a fully specified three-domain mechanism.
emergent_labels_12: Medical Outcomes Study Social Support Measure
conceptual_tensions_1: The paper critiques existing biopsychosocial/PIPT frameworks for missing socioeconomic, ethnocultural, and interpersonal factors while proposing a PIPT model that remains centered on physical therapy interventions
conceptual_tensions_2: The general model is grounded in PIPT evidence, yet the authors state that mediators may differ in CALD populations and must be tested
conceptual_tensions_3: Social factors are central to tailoring and proposed as mediators/moderators, but the core mechanism remains primarily cognitive-emotional and physical
conceptual_tensions_4: The paper calls for culturally relevant care while acknowledging that existing rehabilitation frameworks are vague, difficult to test, and limited to behavioral mechanisms
conceptual_tensions_5: Prayer and remedios are incorporated as culturally relevant coping options alongside evidence-based PIPT techniques
additional_observations_1: This is a perspective/intervention logic model, not an empirical test of the proposed mechanisms
additional_observations_2: The Latino example is operationalized in a Federally Qualified Health Center near the United States-Mexico border
additional_observations_3: The social domain is more developed than in many PIPT papers but functions mainly as tailoring, moderator, mediator, and contextual determinant
additional_observations_4: The paper does not provide formal definitions for most psychological constructs beyond psychological flexibility
additional_observations_5: The article reports no quality-of-evidence appraisal because of its scoping/narrative nature
additional_observations_6: No spiritual/religious framework is developed, prayer is treated as a coping option rather than a formal construct
synthesis_note: The paper operationalizes BPS as a PIPT logic model: physical therapy components plus cognitive-emotional skill training plus sociocultural tailoring. It goes beyond listing domains by specifying mediators/moderators and culturally relevant constructs, but the social domain mainly functions as context/tailoring for a biopsychosocial PIPT mechanism rather than as an independently modeled causal system.
coding_rationale: All three domains are present and linked, but the social domain is mostly a moderator/tailoring layer; therefore triadic integration is partial rather than a fully specified three-way mechanism.

title: Psychologically Informed Physical Therapy Management of Chronic Musculoskeletal Pain in Culturally Diverse Populations: An Intervention Logic Model
authors: Katrina S. Monroe; Kristin R. Archer; Stephen T. Wegener; Sara P. Gombatto
pain_condition_detail: chronic musculoskeletal pain in culturally and linguistically diverse populations
context_note: US-Mexico border health center serving Latino population
bps_function_set: background framing; critique or problematization; explanatory framework; intervention rationale; organizing principle
bps_operationalization_summary: Uses BPS as organizing framework for PIPT interventions but critiques its failure to address social factors. Develops intervention logic model with essential elements for cultural adaptation.
integration_mechanism_summary: none proposed
conceptual_tensions_1: BPS label is used but social domain is critiqued as absent from PIPT practice
conceptual_tensions_2: Psychological constructs are well-developed but lack integration with biological and social domains
conceptual_tensions_3: Cultural adaptation is proposed but mechanisms of cultural influence are not specified
conceptual_tensions_4: Intervention logic model is presented but lacks empirical testing of proposed pathways
additional_observations_1: The paper uses BPS terminology extensively but does not define the model itself, only citing Engel's model as foundation
additional_observations_2: Essential interventions are identified as cognitive skill training, aerobic activity, therapeutic exercise, and functional movement training
additional_observations_3: Cultural adaptation for Latino population includes addressing fatalismo, familismo, and personalismo
additional_observations_4: The logic model proposes psychological flexibility and self-efficacy as key mediators but does not specify biological or social pathways
synthesis_note: This paper uses the biopsychosocial model as an organizing framework for PIPT interventions but critically notes that social factors are rarely addressed in practice. It develops an intervention logic model with four essential elements (cognitive skill training, aerobic activity, therapeutic exercise, functional movement training) and identifies psychological constructs like catastrophizing, fear avoidance, and self-efficacy as key mediators. The paper emphasizes cultural adaptation for Latino populations, incorporating constructs like fatalismo and familismo. However, the BPS integration is superficial - biological and social domains are mentioned but not meaningfully integrated with psychological
coding_rationale: BPS typology is multifactorial because all three domains are present but not integrated. Psychological domain is elaborated with multiple constructs, biological and social are mentioned but not developed. Integration is 'none' because domains are treated in parallel without specified pathways between them.

title: The potential impact of exercise on affect and neuroinflammation in older adults living with fibromyalgia: a scoping review
authors: Taylor L. Taylor; Fitzgerald Dodds; McKenna Tharpe; Emily L. Zumbro; Michael Hankes; Raymond Jones; Deanna Rumble; Lisa Antoine; Kristen Allen-Watts; Andrew Sims; Reshu Chandra; Burel R. Goodin; Jarred Younger; Thomas W. Buford
pain_condition_detail: Fibromyalgia (FM), a widespread chronic pain condition, in older adults aged 65 years or older.
bps_function_set: background framing; conclusion; organizing principle
bps_operationalization_summary: The paper uses the Biopsychosocial Framework of Chronic Pain as an organizing principle to structure the review around affect (psychological) and neuroinflammation (biological), but does not define the model or integrate social factors substantively. The framework is invoked in the abstract and conclusion but not operationalized in methods or results.
integration_mechanism_summary: None proposed. The paper asserts directional relationships between exercise and affect, and between neuroinflammation and affect, but does not specify pathways or mediators. Social factors are mentioned as benefits of exercise but not integrated with biological or psychological domains.
conceptual_tensions_1: The paper claims a biopsychosocial framework but focuses almost exclusively on biological (neuroinflammation) and psychological (affect) domains, with social factors only mentioned in passing
conceptual_tensions_2: The relationship between neuroinflammation and affect is asserted as directional but no mechanism or mediator is specified, leaving the integration claim weak

synthesis_note: This scoping review uses the biopsychosocial label to frame a review of exercise effects on affect and neuroinflammation in older adults with fibromyalgia, but operationalizes only two domains (psychological and biological) with minimal social content. coding_rationale: Typology is pseudo_bps because BPS language is used but social domain is minimal and integration is absent. Triadic integration is none because social domain is not integrated. Psych-dominant because affect outcomes are elaborated while biological and social are thin.

additional_observations_4: It distinguishes neuroinflammation from systemic inflammation but uses both in mechanisms
additional_observations_5: It calls for qualitative approaches to exercise adherence
additional_observations_6: Quality assessments were conducted but not weighted in the scoping review synthesis
synthesis_note: The review operationalizes BPS mainly through exercise, affect, neuroinflammation, and adherence in older adults with FM. It develops biological and psychological mechanisms while social factors remain barriers/context, yielding partial BPS integration.

bps_operationalization_summary: The review uses BPS as an organizing framework to structure its investigation of exercise effects on affect and neuroinflammation in fibromyalgia, but does not integrate the three domains through specified mechanisms or pathways.
integration_mechanism_summary: The paper proposes directional relationships: exercise improves affect and may reduce neuroinflammation; neuroinflammation contributes to depression; fear avoidance and depression create barriers to exercise adherence. A conceptual framework suggests reciprocal relationships between these factors, but no detailed mechanistic pathways are specified.
conceptual_tensions_1: Tension between the BPS framework's promise of integration and the paper's limited empirical evidence for biological outcomes
conceptual_tensions_2: Gap between the conceptual framework's reciprocal relationships and the lack of detailed mechanistic pathways
conceptual_tensions_3: Mismatch between the BPS label and the actual depth of social domain content
additional_observations_1: The review focuses on older adults with fibromyalgia, a specific population within chronic pain
additional_observations_2: Exercise modalities studied include aerobic, resistance, combined, and stretching exercises
additional_observations_3: Quality assessment was conducted but studies were not weighted in conclusions
additional_observations_4: The review acknowledges its own limitations in participant demographics and outcome measurement
synthesis_note: This scoping review operationalizes the biopsychosocial model as an organizing framework to investigate exercise effects on affect and neuroinflammation in older adults with fibromyalgia. While the psychological domain is well-developed with constructs like affective styles and depression, biological content is limited to theoretical mechanisms with sparse empirical evidence. Social domain content is minimal. The review proposes a conceptual framework suggesting reciprocal relationships but lacks detailed mechanistic integration. The BPS label serves primarily as an organizing principle rather than an explanatory framework with specified pathways.
coding_rationale: BPS typology as 'multifactorial' because all three domains are present but not mechanistically integrated. Triadic integration as 'partial' due to conceptual framework suggesting relationships but lacking detailed pathways. Psychological domain scored 'elaborated' due to multiple named constructs and their relationships.

title: Wearable Devices for Supporting Chronic Disease Self-Management: Scoping Review
authors: Taiane de Azevedo Cardoso; Jari Ruokolainen; Wentao Wang; Marie-Pierre Gagnon; Steven Ouellet; Eugène Attisso; Wilfried Supper; Samira Amil; Caroline Rhéaume; Jean-Sébastien Paquette; Christian Chabot; Marie-Claude Laferrière; Maxime Sasseville
pain_condition_detail: Chronic pain; musculoskeletal conditions (osteoporosis, rheumatoid arthritis, systemic lupus erythematosus, ankylosing spondylitis); diabetes, heart failure, cardiovascular conditions, hypertension, COPD, asthma, and multimorbidity.
context_note: Most studies were in North America (United States and Canada), with smaller shares in the United Kingdom, Republic of Korea, China, Netherlands, Spain, and multi-country studies.
bps_function_set: conclusion; organizing principle; policy or practice implication
bps_operationalization_summary: The paper uses BPS as an outcome taxonomy, not a model. It classifies measured outcomes into clinical, behavioral, technology-experience, holistic/biopsychosocial, and health-care-system categories; it reports counts and significance but does not model mechanisms linking domains.
integration_mechanism_summary: The paper proposes a device-centered pathway: physiological data from wearables generate real-time feedback; feedback may be automatic or clinician-mediated; this promotes engagement/adherence to health behaviors and can enter clinical workflows. It does not propose a chronic-pain-specific biopsychosocial mechanism.
conceptual_tensions_1: The paper uses a broad chronic-disease wearable frame while chronic pain is represented by only 6 of 79 studies
conceptual_tensions_2: The BPS label is used to describe outcome categories, but no formal biopsychosocial model or chronic-pain mechanism is provided
conceptual_tensions_3: The review reports measured outcomes and effect direction but does not consider effect sizes
conceptual_tensions_4: Multicomponent behavioral strategy interventions are acknowledged as confounding factors but not considered
conceptual_tensions_5: MMAT quality assessment is reported, but no studies are excluded based on MMAT scores
additional_observations_1: Chronic pain studies used only wearable activity trackers and reported clinical, behavioral, and technology-experience outcomes
additional_observations_2: Most included studies were conducted in North America, especially the United States
additional_observations_3: Wearable activity trackers were the most common device across the review
additional_observations_4: The paper's BPS-related content appears mainly in outcome categorization rather than in chronic-pain theory
additional_observations_5: The review includes chronic disease self-management broadly, not only pain populations
additional_observations_6: Quality assessment was performed, but methodological rigor did not determine inclusion
synthesis_note: This paper contributes a scoping map of wearable-device interventions across chronic diseases, with chronic pain as a small cluster. It operationalizes BPS only by adding a holistic/biopsychosocial outcome category; it does not define the model or propose chronic-pain-specific mechanisms. Most evidence is clinical/behavioral, with social content limited to health-care system outcomes.
coding_rationale: BPS is used as an outcome taxonomy across chronic diseases, not a chronic-pain BPS model. Bio and psych outcomes dominate; social appears mainly as health-care system outcomes. Integration is device-feedback rather than three-domain chronic-pain mechanism.

title: Same patient but different worlds: A state-of-the-art review translating best practice psychosocial care from musculoskeletal care to the orthopaedic context
authors: Marie K. March; Katharine E. Roberts
pain_condition_detail: Persistent/chronic musculoskeletal conditions in elective orthopaedic surgery, informed by musculoskeletal care.
context_note: Elective orthopaedic secondary care in hospital settings, with implementation lessons from primary-care musculoskeletal care and attention to women, culturally diverse and low-literacy communities.
bps_function_set: background framing; explanatory framework; intervention rationale; justification; organizing principle; policy or practice implication
bps_operationalization_summary: The paper operationalizes BPS mainly by translating psychosocial assessment, screening tools, interventions, workforce training, shared decision making, registries and equity implementation into orthopaedic care. It lists biological, psychological and social predictors but does not specify a three-domain mechanism.
integration_mechanism_summary: No detailed cross-domain mechanisms are proposed. The paper mainly states that biological, psychological and social factors predict poor recovery and that psychosocial assessment and intervention should be implemented in orthopaedics; the closest pathway is psychosocial assessment/intervention affecting outcomes.
conceptual_tensions_1: The paper says BPS requires interaction of physical, emotional and social factors, but the substantive review is mainly psychosocial implementation with biological factors mostly listed
conceptual_tensions_2: Screening tools for psychosocial risk are recommended in musculoskeletal care, yet orthopaedics lacks a universal comprehensive patient interview incorporating a biopsychosocial approach
conceptual_tensions_3: Decision aids are presented as shared decision-making tools, but the paper says decision aids without interactive processes have not improved surgical outcomes
conceptual_tensions_4: Multidisciplinary mental health care is recommended, but workforce costs and funding models are barriers
conceptual_tensions_5: Equity is emphasized for women and culturally diverse communities, but the paper says these groups have been excluded from research previously
additional_observations_1: The article is a state-of-the-art implementation review, not an effectiveness synthesis of BPS interventions
additional_observations_2: It uses primary-care musculoskeletal evidence to infer what orthopaedic surgery should implement

title: Same patient but different worlds: A state-of-the-art review translating best practice psychosocial care from musculoskeletal care to the orthopaedic context
authors: Marie K. March; Katharine E. Roberts
pain_condition_detail: chronic musculoskeletal conditions and elective orthopaedic surgery outcomes
context_note: Global perspective with specific attention to orthopaedic surgery contexts in primary and secondary care
bps_function_set: background framing; organizing principle; policy or practice implication
bps_operationalization_summary: Organizes the review around psychosocial care implementation in orthopaedic surgery, using BPS as a framing concept to structure discussion of barriers and solutions across multiple levels of healthcare delivery
integration_mechanism_summary: none proposed
conceptual_tensions_1: Tension between BPS theoretical integration and actual parallel listing of domains without specified mechanisms
conceptual_tensions_2: Uncertainty about psychological resilience definition and measurement utility in musculoskeletal contexts
conceptual_tensions_3: Gap between evidence of psychosocial factor associations and actual implementation of psychosocial care approaches in orthopaedic surgery
additional_observations_1: The review focuses primarily on psychological and social factors with minimal biological content, suggesting a psychosocial rather than fully biopsychosocial approach
additional_observations_2: Implementation barriers are discussed at multiple levels (individual, workforce, health service, societal) but without explicit integration mechanisms connecting these levels
additional_observations_3: The review emphasizes practical implementation challenges over theoretical integration of the BPS model
synthesis_note: This scoping review uses the biopsychosocial model as an organizing framework to explore psychosocial care implementation in orthopaedic surgery. It identifies psychological and social factors (depression, anxiety, catastrophizing, kinesiophobia, health literacy, compensation status, cultural diversity) but treats biological factors minimally. The review demonstrates multifactorial typology with no explicit integration mechanisms between domains, representing a gap between BPS theory and practical implementation in surgical contexts.
coding_rationale: Psychological and social domains scored elaborated due to multiple named constructs; biological scored mentioned due to limited constructs. Integration scored 'none' as domains listed in parallel without specified pathways. BPS typology 'multifactorial' as all three domains present but not integrated.

bps_operationalization_summary: The paper uses 'biopsychosocial' once in the abstract as a descriptor of burden. It does not define the model, cite a source, or use it to structure the review. The review is organized around pain-related, physiological, and psychological outcomes without invoking the BPS model analytically.
integration_mechanism_summary: The paper asserts that psychological factors (catastrophizing, depression, anxiety) contribute to central sensitization, but no pathway or mechanism is specified. No integration between psychological and social, biological and social, or triadic domains is proposed.
conceptual_tensions_1: The paper uses 'biopsychosocial' once but does not define it, cite a source, or use it to structure the review
conceptual_tensions_2: Psychological domain is elaborated with multiple constructs and instruments, but social domain is limited to one mention of social support
conceptual_tensions_3: Directional claims (e.g., catastrophizing contributes to central sensitization) are made without specifying a pathway or mechanism
additional_observations_1: The review compares FM and LBP on pain-related, physiological, and psychological outcomes but does not integrate these domains into a biopsychosocial account
additional_observations_2: The paper identifies methodological heterogeneity in definitions and instruments as a limitation, which is relevant to operationalization of constructs
synthesis_note: This scoping review compares FM and LBP on pain-related, physiological, and psychological outcomes. It uses 'biopsychosocial' once in the abstract without definition or integration. Psychological domain is elaborated; social domain is minimal. No triadic integration is proposed. The paper contributes to the question by showing how BPS language can be tokenistic even in a review that compares two chronic pain conditions.
coding_rationale: Typology is pseudo_bps because BPS label is used but social domain is minimal and no integration is present. Triadic integration is none because domains are listed in parallel. Psychological domain is elaborated with multiple constructs and instruments.

citation: Couëpel et al. (2024), BMC Rheumatology
title: What are the functional and clinical characteristics shared by fibromyalgia and low back pain? A scoping review
authors: Bastien Couëpel; Mathieu Tremblay; Marjorie Bernier; Jacques Abboud; Martin Descarreaux
pain_condition_detail: fibromyalgia and chronic primary/non-specific low back pain
context_note: Included studies covered multiple countries; review restricted to English/French publications and three databases.
bps_function_set: background framing; justification; organizing principle
bps_operationalization_summary: BPS label is used to frame burden and organize comparison across pain-related, physiological, and psychological outcomes; the review does not define or model interactions among domains.
integration_mechanism_summary: The paper proposes psychological symptoms may contribute to central sensitization, central sensitization may predict widespread pain, and the relation with widespread pain may be bidirectional. No social-domain pathway is proposed.
conceptual_tensions_1: The paper uses biopsychosocial burden while leaving the model undefined and unmechanized
conceptual_tensions_2: LBP definitions are inconsistent across included studies
conceptual_tensions_3: ACR criteria differ across studies and may select more severe FM cases
conceptual_tensions_4: Measurement heterogeneity and missing minimal clinically important differences limit synthesis
conceptual_tensions_5: The proposed psychological-to-widespread-pain pathway is explicitly bidirectional and unknown
additional_observations_1: No formal risk-of-bias or quality appraisal of included studies is reported
additional_observations_2: Included study designs were mostly cross-sectional, limiting claims about progression from LBP to FM
additional_observations_3: The search was restricted to English/French publications and three databases
additional_observations_4: The social domain appears mainly as social support and socioeconomic descriptors, not as a modeled determinant
synthesis_note: The paper operationalizes BPS as a comparative framework rather than an integrated explanatory model. Biological and psychological mechanisms are discussed, especially central sensitization and affect/cognition, but social content is reduced to socioeconomic context and social support.
coding_rationale: Bio and psych are elaborated; social is mentioned. Bio-psych integration is mechanistic; triadic integration is partial because social factors are not tied into the mechanism. Typology is multifactorial.

title: Insecure Attachment, Oxytocinergic System and C-Tactile Fibers: An Integrative and Translational Pathophysiological Model of Fibromyalgia and Central Sensitivity Syndromes
authors: Gianluca Bruti; Paola Foggetti; Alessandro Rimessi

bps_operationalization_summary: The paper uses the biopsychosocial model as an explanatory framework to integrate attachment system, C-tactile fibers, and oxytocinergic system dysfunction into a pathophysiological model of fibromyalgia and central sensitivity syndromes. It proposes a mechanistic pathway linking early attachment, CT fiber stimulation, and oxytocinergic programming to stress system dysregulation and central sensitization. The model is described narratively without formal operationalization of BPS domains.
integration_mechanism_summary: The paper proposes a mechanistic pathway: insecure attachment and early stress lead to dysfunction of C-tactile fibers and oxytocinergic system, which dysregulates the HPA axis and autonomic nervous system, resulting in central sensitization and chronic pain. This integrates biological (CT fibers, OS, HPA) and psychological (attachment, stress) domains mechanistically, but social factors are only descriptively linked.

additional_observations_2: The review is a narrative synthesis that cites empirical studies but does not conduct a systematic search or quality assessment
additional_observations_3: The term 'biopsychosocial' is used in the abstract and discussion but the paper's actual content is heavily weighted toward biological and psychological mechanisms, with social factors receiving only brief mentions
synthesis_note: This narrative review proposes an integrative pathophysiological model of fibromyalgia linking insecure attachment, C-tactile fiber dysfunction, and oxytocinergic system dysregulation to central sensitization. It uses the biopsychosocial label but operationalizes it as a dyadic bio-psych model with minimal social content. The model is mechanistic for bio-psych integration but social factors are only descriptively linked. The paper contributes a novel theoretical synthesis but does not empirically test or operationalize the model.

citation: Bruti et al. (2024), Biomedicines
title: Insecure Attachment, Oxytocinergic System and C-Tactile Fibers: An Integrative and Translational Pathophysiological Model of Fibromyalgia and Central Sensitivity Syndromes
authors: Gianluca Bruti; Paola Foggetti; Alessandro Rimessi
pain_condition_detail: fibromyalgia syndrome and central sensitivity syndromes
bps_function_set: background framing; explanatory framework; organizing principle
bps_operationalization_summary: The paper uses the biopsychosocial model as an organizing framework to structure its discussion of fibromyalgia pathophysiology, integrating biological (attachment system, CT fibers, oxytocin), psychological (stress response, threat system), and social (caregiving, bio-behavioral synchrony) factors without formally defining the model itself.
integration_mechanism_summary: The paper proposes a mechanistic triadic model where insecure attachment and early life stress dysregulate the attachment system and oxytocinergic system through altered bio-behavioral synchrony, leading to threat system hyperactivity and soothing system dysfunction, which together drive central sensitization and chronic pain.
bps_model_variants_1: biopsychosocial model of chronic pain syndromes
conceptual_tensions_1: The proposed 'Threat and Soothing Systems' model is criticized as not truly novel but rather a restatement of ANS dysregulation without incorporating recent findings on small fibers and immune mechanisms
conceptual_tensions_2: The paper uses the biopsychosocial label extensively but does not provide a formal definition of what the model means in this context
additional_observations_1: The paper presents a comprehensive integrative model linking early attachment experiences to chronic pain through neurobiological pathways involving CT fibers and oxytocin
additional_observations_2: The model emphasizes the developmental programming of stress response systems during the sensitive period of early life
additional_observations_3: The paper integrates findings from psychology, neuroscience, and social biology to explain fibromyalgia pathophysiology
synthesis_note: This paper provides a detailed integrative model of fibromyalgia pathophysiology that genuinely integrates biological, psychological, and social domains through mechanistic pathways. It uses the biopsychosocial model as an organizing framework but does not formally define it. The paper proposes that insecure attachment and early life stress dysregulate the attachment system and oxytocinergic system, leading to threat-soothing imbalance and central sensitization. While the integration is mechanistic, the paper acknowledges limitations in its model's novelty and comprehensiveness.
coding_rationale: The paper demonstrates true triadic integration with mechanistic pathways linking attachment, CT fibers, and oxytocin systems to stress response and central sensitization. The BPS model serves as an explanatory framework without formal definition. Integration is rated mechanistic based on explicit causal pathways proposed between all three domains.

synthesis_note: This scoping review uses BPS as an intervention rationale and organizing principle for eHealth multimodal interventions in older adults. pain_condition_detail: Chronic noncancer pain in older adults, including osteoarthritis/knee osteoarthritis, chronic low back pain, chronic musculoskeletal pain, and sciatica.
context_note: Included studies were from the United States, Germany, the United Kingdom, Canada, Australia, and Thailand; many recruited participants from community-based settings.
bps_function_set: background framing; explanatory framework; intervention rationale; justification; organizing principle; policy or practice implication
bps_operationalization_summary: The review operationalizes BPS mainly by requiring eHealth interventions to combine physical and psychosocial components and by grouping outcomes into pain, psychological, physical, integrated biopsychosocial, and other categories. It synthesizes content and outcomes narratively but does not model cross-domain mechanisms.
integration_mechanism_summary: None proposed. The paper describes BPS as an interaction and lists physical, psychological, and social content or outcomes, but it does not specify mediators, moderators, or cross-domain processes.
quality_assessment_tools_1: quality assessment tool for studies with diverse designs (qatsdd)
bps_model_variants_2: biopsychosocial multimodal approach to CNCP management
conceptual_tensions_1: The paper invokes a BPS interaction but operationalizes it mainly as co-presence of physical and psychosocial components
conceptual_tensions_2: Social content appears as support or context rather than as a mechanism, despite social functioning and social participation being listed
conceptual_tensions_3: The review casts older adults as heterogeneous, but the evidence is concentrated in 65- to 75-year-olds
conceptual_tensions_4: Digital health is framed as improving access, while social support, family/caregiver help, and face-to-face care remain important
conceptual_tensions_5: Pain outcomes rely on self-report and numeric ratings, while the paper notes subjective interpretation and peak-end bias
additional_observations_1: The review excludes stand-alone physical and stand-alone psychosocial eHealth interventions, so the BPS frame is enforced at inclusion rather than analyzed as a mechanism
additional_observations_2: Outcomes are grouped as pain, psychological, physical, integrated biopsychosocial, and other, but pairwise links are mostly listed rather than modeled
additional_observations_3: eHealth delivery is heterogeneous: web-based programs, mHealth, teleconsulting/video consulting, VR, email, websites, smartphone apps, and wearable activity monitors
additional_observations_4: No spiritual or existential constructs are named
additional_observations_5: The article uses QATSDD but not AMSTAR, ROBIS, GRADE, or Cochrane risk of bias
additional_observations_6: Self-determination needs are named without naming self-determination theory
synthesis_note: This review operationalizes BPS mostly as an inclusion criterion for eHealth interventions combining physical and psychosocial components and as an outcome taxonomy. It names biological, psychological, and social content, but social factors are contextual and cross-domain links are mostly listed rather than modeled.
coding_rationale: BPS label frames scope and intervention content; biological, psychological, and social domains are present but parallel, with no specified mechanism, so multifactorial.

title: eHealth-Integrated Psychosocial and Physical Interventions for Chronic Pain in Older Adults: Scoping Review
authors: Taiane de Azevedo Cardoso; Leo Benning; Deepak Singh; Annalisa De Lucia; Cinzia Perlini; Alessandro Chiarotto; Sara Pachera; Ilenia Pasini; Lidia Del Piccolo; Valeria Donisi
pain_condition_detail: chronic noncancer pain in older adults
context_note: International studies from US, Europe, Canada, Australia, Thailand
bps_function_set: background framing; conclusion; organizing principle
bps_operationalization_summary: The review uses BPS as an organizing principle to structure multimodal eHealth interventions combining physical and psychosocial components, but does not specify mechanisms of integration between domains.
integration_mechanism_summary: none proposed
quality_assessment_tools_1: quality assessment tool for studies with diverse designs
conceptual_tensions_1: Tension between BPS labeling and actual domain integration - domains are listed in parallel without specified mechanisms of interaction
conceptual_tensions_2: Limited representation of social factors - only 1 study considers family involvement despite its importance for older adults' eHealth adoption
conceptual_tensions_3: Biological factors treated as contextual rather than active constructs in the intervention design
additional_observations_1: The review maps eHealth multimodal interventions but does not critically examine the BPS model's operationalization
additional_observations_2: Interventions combine physical and psychosocial components through parallel module structure rather than integrated mechanisms
additional_observations_3: Quality assessment used QATSDD tool with studies rated medium to high quality
additional_observations_4: No study assessed frailty despite its relevance for older adults with chronic pain
synthesis_note: This scoping review maps eHealth multimodal interventions for chronic pain in older adults, using the biopsychosocial label as an organizing principle. The review finds that interventions combine physical and psychosocial components in parallel modules without specifying integration mechanisms between domains. Psychological constructs are well-developed (self-efficacy, catastrophizing, acceptance, kinesiophobia), while biological factors are mentioned only as contextual conditions and social factors minimally. The BPS label serves as background framing and organizational structure rather than an explanatory framework with mechanistic integration.
coding_rationale: BPS typology is 'multifactorial' because all three domains are present but treated in parallel without integration mechanisms. Psychological domain is 'elaborated' with 10 named constructs, biological is 'mentioned' with 3 contextual factors, social is 'mentioned' with 3 outcome measures. Integration is 'none' as no cross-domain pathways are specified.

title: The emergence of sex differences in primary pain during adolescence: a conceptual developmentally-oriented biopsychosocial model and opportunities for further investigation
authors: Hannah Hagy; Esmeralda Hidalgo-Lopez; Christel Portengen; Alexis Holman; Andrew Schrepf; Daniel J. Clauw; Steven E. Harte; Adriene M. Beltz; Amy M. Bohnert; Chelsea M. Kaplan
pain_condition_detail: primary pain conditions including fibromyalgia, migraine/headache, temporomandibular disorder, irritable bowel syndrome, chronic pelvic pain, multisite pain
bps_function_set: background framing; conclusion; explanatory framework; organizing principle
bps_operationalization_summary: The paper uses the BPS label to organize a narrative review of sex differences in primary pain during adolescence. It lists biological, behavioral, cognitive-affective, and sociocultural factors as overlapping contributors, with brain network function as a central susceptibility factor. No empirical integration or testing of the model is performed.
integration_mechanism_summary: The paper proposes that brain network function is a central susceptibility factor that interacts with overlapping biological, behavioral, cognitive-affective, and sociocultural factors. Specific directional claims include hormones reorganizing brain regions and adverse events influencing pubertal timing. No mechanistic triadic pathway is specified.
conceptual_tensions_1: The paper lists biological, behavioral, cognitive-affective, and sociocultural factors as overlapping but does not specify how they interact mechanistically
conceptual_tensions_2: Sex and gender are acknowledged as distinct but the paper largely focuses on sex due to its neurobiological focus, leaving the role of gender underexplored
conceptual_tensions_3: The model proposes brain network function as a central susceptibility factor, but the evidence for this is limited to one study in children prior to pain onset
additional_observations_1: The paper emphasizes the need for sex-stratified analyses and consideration of pubertal status, timing, and tempo in future research
additional_observations_2: The review is conceptual and not exhaustive, aiming to provide a broad overview rather than a systematic synthesis
synthesis_note: This conceptual review proposes a developmentally-oriented biopsychosocial model to explain sex differences in primary pain during adolescence. It provides a broad overview of biological, behavioral, cognitive-affective, and sociocultural factors, with a strong emphasis on brain network function and pubertal hormones. However, it does not empirically integrate these factors or specify mechanistic pathways, resulting in a multifactorial rather than integrative use of the BPS model.
coding_rationale: Typology is multifactorial because all three domains are present but treated in parallel with no mechanistic integration. Triadic integration is partial because brain network function is linked to multiple factors but no specific pathway is specified. Bio-dominant due to extensive coverage of hormones, brain structure, and nociplastic mechanisms.

citation: Hagy et al. (2025), BMC Pediatrics
title: The emergence of sex differences in primary pain during adolescence: a conceptual developmentally-oriented biopsychosocial model and opportunities for further investigation
authors: Hannah Hagy; Esmeralda Hidalgo-Lopez; Christel Portengen; Alexis Holman; Andrew Schrepf; Daniel J. Clauw; Steven E. Harte; Adriene M. Beltz; Amy M. Bohnert; Chelsea M. Kaplan
pain_condition_detail: Primary pain/chronic overlapping pain conditions in adolescents and youth, with emphasis on sex and gender differences emerging during puberty.
context_note: NIH sex-as-biological-variable policy; no specific healthcare system reported.
bps_function_set: background framing; explanatory framework; intervention rationale; organizing principle; policy or practice implication
bps_usage_sections: abstract; conclusion; other; table or figure
bps_operationalization_summary: The paper uses BPS as a developmental organizing frame: puberty/CNS mechanisms are linked with behavioral, cognitive-affective, and sociocultural factors to explain female-biased primary pain, but it does not define a formal model or specify a complete causal pathway.
integration_mechanism_summary: Proposed pathways are mostly hypothesized: puberty hormones alter CNS structure/function and pain modulation; sleep and activity interact with CNS connectivity; attention/emotion regulation and sociocultural exposures shape pain reporting, symptoms, and help-seeking. No complete causal model is specified.
conceptual_tensions_1: Sex and gender are described as distinct but difficult to disentangle in primary pain development
conceptual_tensions_2: The model integrates biology, behavior, cognition-affect, and sociocultural factors, but mechanisms remain largely unknown
conceptual_tensions_3: Puberty can be measured as status, timing, or tempo, yet these aspects are often confounded or poorly specified
conceptual_tensions_4: Sex differences can be quantitative, qualitative, latent, or population-based, but many studies control sex rather than model these types
conceptual_tensions_5: Pain is framed as primary/nociplastic without peripheral pathology, yet nociplastic processes can amplify nociceptive pain
additional_observations_1: The paper is explicitly conceptual, not a pooled evidence synthesis, it synthesizes pediatric pain, neuroimaging, and adolescent-development literatures
additional_observations_2: The BPS frame is operationalized through domain headings and future measurement guidance for puberty rather than through named validated pain instruments
additional_observations_3: Female puberty, hormones, and CNS development are foregrounded, research on gender-expansive individuals and sex as a continuum is explicitly noted as lacking
additional_observations_4: The model foregrounds equifinality: no single factor is enough to explain sex differences in primary pain for all youth
additional_observations_5: Precision-treatment recommendations are made without specifying a concrete multimodal intervention
additional_observations_6: Many cross-domain claims are framed as hypotheses or gaps, not as tested effects
synthesis_note: This paper operationalizes BPS as a developmental explanatory model for adolescent primary pain: puberty/hormones and CNS are linked with sleep/activity, attention/emotion regulation, and sociocultural exposures to explain female-biased pain. It is integrative but largely hypothetical, with several named gaps and no tested causal model.
coding_rationale: BPS label is explanatory/organizing; all three domains are substantive and linked through puberty/CNS hypotheses, though no formal definition or tested pathway is specified.

authors: Hannah Hagy; Esmeralda Hidalgo-Lopez; Christel Portengen; Alexis Holman; Andrew Schrepf; Daniel J. Clauw; Steven E. Harte; Adriene M. Beltz; Amy M. Bohnert; Chelsea M. Kaplan

bps_operationalization_summary: Organizes review around four BPS domains (biological, behavioral, cognitive-affective, sociocultural) with brain networks as susceptibility factor. No formal integration mechanism specified; domains presented as parallel factors contributing to sex differences in primary pain during puberty.
integration_mechanism_summary: none proposed
conceptual_tensions_1: Tension between BPS language usage and actual mechanistic integration - paper uses BPS label extensively but does not specify how domains interact mechanistically
conceptual_tensions_2: Tension between acknowledging sex/gender as important while noting they are difficult to disentangle - paper states both that sex and gender matter and that disentangling their roles is difficult
conceptual_tensions_3: Tension between proposing brain networks as susceptibility factors while acknowledging mechanisms are largely unknown - central hypothesis lacks empirical support
conceptual_tensions_4: Tension between recommending sex-stratified analyses while most existing studies use single-sex cohorts or control for sex
additional_observations_1: The paper distinguishes between four types of sex differences: quantitative, qualitative, latent, and population-based, each requiring different analytical approaches
additional_observations_2: Focus on adolescence as a 'pivotal period' emphasizes developmental timing rather than static individual differences
additional_observations_3: The review is explicitly conceptual/theoretical rather than empirical, building on existing literature rather than presenting new data
additional_observations_4: Gender is acknowledged as non-binary and existing research predominantly uses binary operationalization, creating a gap for gender-expansive individuals
synthesis_note: This conceptual review uses the biopsychosocial label as an organizing principle to structure discussion of sex/gender differences in primary pain during adolescence. It identifies biological (hormones, CNS), psychological (cognitive-affective factors), and social (gendered experiences, adverse events) factors but does not specify mechanistic integration between domains. The paper's main contribution is highlighting methodological gaps in puberty measurement and sex-stratified analysis rather than providing an integrated BPS framework.
coding_rationale: BPS typology is 'multifactorial' because all three domains are substantively present but treated in parallel without specified integration mechanisms. Triadic integration is 'none' because no cross-domain pathways are specified. Domain coverage is 'elaborated' for all three core domains based on multiple named constructs per domain.

title: Comorbidities Across Functional Neurological Disorder Subtypes: A Comprehensive Narrative Synthesis
authors: Ioannis Mavroudis; Katerina Franekova; Foivos Petridis; Alin Ciobîca; Dăscălescu Gabriel; Emil Anton; Ciprian Ilea; Sotirios Papagiannopoulos; Dimitrios Kazis; Katalin Prokai-Tatrai
pain_condition_detail: Functional neurological disorder (FND) and subtypes: Functional Cognitive Disorder (FCD), Functional Movement Disorder (FMD), Psychogenic Non-Epileptic Seizures (PNES), Persistent Postural-Perceptual Dizziness (PPPD), general/mixed FND, with chronic pain and fibromyalgia comorbidities.
context_note: United Kingdom population estimate; higher rates in industrialized nations; limited cross-ethnic research; diverse groups named including African American, Pacific Islander, Asian, Caucasian, European.
bps_function_set: background framing; conclusion; explanatory framework; intervention rationale; justification; policy or practice implication
bps_operationalization_summary: Uses BPS as a broad explanatory frame for FND comorbidities; organizes evidence by psychiatric versus somatic comorbidity and FND subtype; links biological mechanisms, psychological trauma/stress/cognition, and social context/access. Mostly descriptive clustering and integrated-care rationale, not a specified three-domain mechanism.
integration_mechanism_summary: No explicit triadic mechanism. Proposed pathways are mostly subtype-level: neural circuit/network dysfunction, interoception/central sensitization, trauma/stress/dissociation, attentional bias, maladaptive beliefs, and social/contextual barriers. PPPD has a behavioral loop, but the social domain remains background.
conceptual_tensions_1: FND is described as lacking structural abnormality, yet the review emphasizes network dysfunction and biomarkers
conceptual_tensions_2: The BPS prism is invoked, but social context is mostly epidemiology, culture, and access rather than an analytic mediator
conceptual_tensions_3: Psychiatric comorbidities dominate several sections, while somatic and pain comorbidities are presented as overlapping but less developed
conceptual_tensions_4: FCD is framed as functional despite overlap with dementia and mild cognitive impairment
conceptual_tensions_5: PRISMA-style selection is used, but the paper states it is not a strict systematic review
additional_observations_1: The paper uses both biopsychological and biopsychosocial vocabulary
additional_observations_2: Comorbidity classification is psychiatric versus somatic/medical, not BPS domains
additional_observations_3: The strongest triadic language appears in the introduction and conclusion, but causal pathways are mostly within bio-psych subdomains
additional_observations_4: PPPD is the clearest example of a behavioral loop involving vestibular instability, hypervigilance, attentional focus, and cognitive schemas
additional_observations_5: Future research calls for longitudinal causal studies, biomarkers, and culturally diverse cohorts
additional_observations_6: No formal BPS definition or operational coding scheme is provided
synthesis_note: This review operationalizes BPS mainly as a broad frame for FND comorbidity rather than a coded model. It substantively covers psychiatric constructs and neurobiological mechanisms, while social content is mostly context, culture, access, and gaps. Cross-domain links are mostly descriptive subtype clustering or care recommendations, with limited explicit three-domain mechanism.
coding_rationale: Psych-dominant: psychiatric comorbidities and mechanisms receive most detail; neurobiology is developed, social content thinner. BPS is descriptive/integrative in language, not fully mechanistic triad.

bps_operationalization_summary: Organizes findings by FND subtypes and comorbidity categories, using BPS language to frame how biological, psychological, and social factors interact to produce symptoms, but does not operationalize the model into specific variables or measures.
integration_mechanism_summary: The paper proposes descriptive triadic interaction where biological vulnerability, psychological factors, and social context jointly influence FND symptoms, with directional relationships between biological factors and symptoms, psychiatric comorbidities and treatment outcomes, trauma and PNES, social determinants and vulnerability, and stigma and diagnostic delay. pain_condition_detail: Persistent postpartum genitopelvic or postsurgical pain, urinary incontinence, functional ability, and postpartum mental health outcomes.
context_note: The review frames maternal morbidity as a public health issue and includes English- or Dutch-language studies, but does not report a single country or healthcare system.
bps_function_set: background framing; conclusion; intervention rationale; organizing principle; policy or practice implication
bps_operationalization_summary: It operationalizes BPS mainly through ICF: recovery outcomes are grouped into physical, mental, functional, and social participation domains, and factors into seven antenatal/pregnancy categories. The paper reports associations and recommends tailored care, but it does not define BPS variables, test a model, or specify cross-domain mechanisms.
integration_mechanism_summary: None proposed. The paper reports associations and recommends combining exercise, mental health support, and workplace adaptations, but does not specify a biological, psychological, or social pathway linking them.
bps_model_variants_3: biopsychosocial approach to antenatal and postpartum care
conceptual_tensions_1: The review’s BPS/ICF framing includes social participation, but no included studies assessed it
conceptual_tensions_2: Physical recovery is the most frequently assessed domain, while functional ability and social participation are underrepresented
conceptual_tensions_3: Physical activity is protective in some included studies but null or adverse in others
conceptual_tensions_4: Age thresholds and outcome definitions vary, limiting comparability across studies
conceptual_tensions_5: Biomedical outcomes dominate despite the stated aim to assess recovery as multidimensional
additional_observations_1: The ICF framework organizes outcomes into physical, mental, functional, and social participation domains, BPS is not converted into measured variables
additional_observations_2: Narrative synthesis was used because study heterogeneity precluded meta-analysis
additional_observations_3: The paper treats lifestyle as a separate category rather than as a pathway linking biological, psychological, and social domains
additional_observations_4: Quality assessment used NOS and RoB 2, no AMSTAR, ROBIS, or GRADE tool is named
additional_observations_5: Social support is framed as potentially modifiable, but only one eligible study evaluated it
additional_observations_6: The paper recommends combining prenatal exercise, mental health support, and workplace adaptations without specifying how these components interact
synthesis_note: The review uses ICF to operationalize a multidimensional recovery frame and groups factors into biomedical, psychological, social, and lifestyle categories. It reports many associations, especially psychological predictors of pain/functional outcomes, but does not define a BPS mechanism or test variables; social participation is absent from included evidence.
coding_rationale: Domains are mostly parallel, with strongest psych-bio and psych-social associations. Social participation is underrepresented. No triadic mechanism is specified.

Psychological domain is elaborated through multiple constructs; biological and social are mentioned but not linked. title: Acoustic stimulation in pain management: neurobiological mechanisms and clinical applications—a narrative review
authors: Jianbo Song; Heng Zhang; Linzhi Wu; Zhengjin Duan; Ge Luo; Meihui Li; Lin He
pain_condition_detail: Acute and chronic pain across perioperative, procedural, cancer, fibromyalgia, low back/neck pain, migraines, phantom limb pain, postherpetic neuralgia, and diabetic peripheral neuropathy.
context_note: Eligibility included all ages, geographical locations, and ethnicities; no specific healthcare system was specified.
bps_function_set: background framing; justification; rhetorical label
bps_operationalization_summary: The BPS term is used only to acknowledge pain has biopsychosocial dimensions; the review then operationalizes pain relief through acoustic stimulation mechanisms—CNS, ANS, immune/endocrine, and neurochemical pathways—and clinical AS modalities, with social factors mostly contextual.
integration_mechanism_summary: No true triadic BPS mechanism is proposed. The strongest cross-domain pathway is bio-psychological: AS modulates CNS, autonomic, inflammatory, and endocrine mechanisms that are linked to cognitive processing, anxiety, affect, and pain outcomes. Social factors are mostly contextual moderators or implementation barriers.
conceptual_tensions_1: The paper invokes biopsychosocial dimensions but operationalizes the review mainly through neurobiological mechanisms
conceptual_tensions_2: AS is defined as auditory/somatosensory acoustic stimulation, yet immersive VR/AR/MR technologies are included because they integrate acoustic information
conceptual_tensions_3: Acoustic components in immersive technologies are often embedded but not methodologically specified
conceptual_tensions_4: Evidence is concentrated in perioperative pain, fibromyalgia, chronic back pain, and phantom limb pain, while neuropathic pain is sparse
conceptual_tensions_5: Multisensory audiovisual interventions raise placebo and blinding concerns
additional_observations_1: No effect sizes are pooled and no meta-analysis is conducted, the synthesis is narrative despite naming future quality tools
additional_observations_2: The review includes basic research mechanisms and clinical trials/observational studies across all ages and geographies
additional_observations_3: Social factors appear mainly as moderators or implementation barriers rather than explanatory mechanisms
additional_observations_4: Psychological constructs are mostly outcomes or mediators, not a developed analytic domain
additional_observations_5: The conclusion calls for neuroimaging, biochemical markers, and QST to make mechanisms objective
synthesis_note: This review is a neurobiological narrative review that briefly invokes BPS language but does not operationalize BPS as a three-domain model. It codes acoustic stimulation through CNS, autonomic, immune/endocrine, and neurochemical mechanisms, with psychological constructs mostly as pain/affect outcomes or mediators. Social factors are sparse implementation/contextual moderators, so it exemplifies narrow-despite-label use.
coding_rationale: BPS is explicit but undefined and not used to organize analysis; biological content dominates, psych is present as mechanisms/outcomes, social is thin. Bio-psych integration is mechanistic; triadic integration is only partial.

pain_condition_detail: Nociceptive, neuropathic, and nociplastic pain.

bps_function_set: background framing; explanatory framework; intervention rationale; justification; organizing principle; policy or practice implication
bps_operationalization_summary: Uses BPS as an organizing and explanatory frame for pain mechanisms, risk factors, and multimodal care. It operationalizes BPS mainly through nociceptive/neuropathic/nociplastic taxonomy and biological treatment pathways; psychological and social content is present but less developed.
integration_mechanism_summary: The paper proposes biological vulnerabilities/injury, stressors/lifestyle, and psychological factors converging on maladaptive neuroplasticity/homeostasis, with a childhood-adversity→catastrophizing pathway. It does not specify a detailed social-to-biological mediator.
conceptual_tensions_1: The abstract presents a systematic synthesis, while the limitations state that the paper is a narrative review, not a systematic review or meta-analysis
conceptual_tensions_2: The BPS frame promises biological, psychological, and social integration, but the paper is dominated by biological mechanism and treatment taxonomy
conceptual_tensions_3: CAP is presented as transformative, yet the paper notes it has not been exhaustively studied for pain relief as a primary endpoint
conceptual_tensions_4: The hippocampus model combines conventional neurobiology with higher-dimensional and Akashic Records language, creating a tension between mechanistic and metaphysical framing
conceptual_tensions_5: Precision pain medicine depends on biomarkers, but the review states that no single definitive biomarker currently diagnoses pain mechanisms
additional_observations_1: The paper uses nociplastic pain as a mechanistic category rather than mapping it directly onto ICD-11 chronic primary pain
additional_observations_2: Psychological constructs are mostly used as therapy targets or risk factors rather than being operationalized through named instruments
additional_observations_3: Social content is thin and mostly limited to support, stressors, adversity, and broad social determinants
additional_observations_4: The BPS operationalization is strongest in the nociplastic pain treatment section
additional_observations_5: CAP and the hippocampus sensor model are original frontiers that may expand the apparent BPS breadth without adding conventional social content
additional_observations_6: No formal quality or risk-of-bias assessment is reported
synthesis_note: The paper invokes BPS as a broad explanatory frame for chronic pain mechanisms and multimodal care, but operationalizes it mainly through mechanism-based nociceptive/neuropathic/nociplastic taxonomy and biological risk/treatment pathways. Psychological factors are named and used in therapy rationale; social content is thin, mainly support/stressors/social determinants. Triadic integration is mostly co-action/synergy rather than a detailed mechanism.
coding_rationale: BPS language is explicit but mostly organizing/explanatory. Biology is elaborated; psych and social are thinner; lifestyle is developed. Triadic integration is descriptive because synergy is asserted, not fully specified.

Psychological factors are elaborated (resilience, depression, catastrophizing, fear-avoidance), while biological and social factors are mentioned but not developed. title: Biopsychosocial and Cultural Determinants of Functioning and Healthcare Outcomes in Chronic Non-Cancer Pain: An Integrative Review
authors: Rocío Cáceres-Matos; Miguel Garrido-Bueno; Juan Manuel Fernández-Sarmiento; Ana María Porcel-Gálvez; Manuel Pabón-Carrasco; Daniele Giansanti
pain_condition_detail: Chronic non-cancer pain (CNCP) in adults, including musculoskeletal, widespread, and other persistent pain conditions.
context_note: Studies published in English and Spanish, with some focus on rural populations and gender differences.
bps_function_set: background framing; conclusion; explanatory framework; organizing principle
bps_operationalization_summary: Organizes findings into five thematic domains (biological, functioning/QoL, psychological, social support, social/gender determinants) and argues for their interaction within a BPS framework, though integration is described rather than mechanistically specified.
integration_mechanism_summary: The paper proposes a descriptive triadic integration where biological vulnerability, psychological regulation, functional capacity, and social context continuously shape one another reciprocally. Directional relationships are specified between domains, but no mechanistic pathways are detailed.
conceptual_tensions_1: Tension between academic recognition of BPS multidimensional nature and clinical practice's continued biomedical focus
conceptual_tensions_2: Tension between descriptive triadic integration and lack of mechanistic pathways explaining domain interactions
conceptual_tensions_3: Tension between evidence on social determinants and their underrepresentation in existing literature
conceptual_tensions_4: Tension between cross-sectional study designs limiting causal inference and the need for longitudinal understanding of BPS interactions
additional_observations_1: The review uses integrative methodology to synthesize both quantitative and qualitative evidence through convergent thematic synthesis
additional_observations_2: Gender is treated as a cross-cutting determinant with specific mention of gender-based discrimination and women's experience of pain as 'bodily protest'
additional_observations_3: Rural residence is identified as a specific contextual factor associated with higher CNCP prevalence
additional_observations_4: The review explicitly excludes cancer-related pain and cognitive impairment populations, focusing specifically on CNCP in adults
additional_observations_5: Cultural aspects are interpreted as 'socially shared meanings and norms through which chronic pain is understood and experienced'
synthesis_note: This review provides a comprehensive synthesis of CNCP evidence using an integrative approach, explicitly framing the condition through a biopsychosocial lens. It elaborates all three core domains with substantial constructs and identifies directional relationships between them, though integration remains descriptive rather than mechanistic. The review identifies key conceptual problems including underrepresentation of social determinants and healthcare quality, and a gap between academic recognition and clinical implementation of BPS principles. The evidence base is strengthened by systematic appraisal using SIGN and JBI tools, though limitations include cross-sectional designs and high-income country
coding_rationale: Scored as 'elaborated' for all three core domains based on multiple named constructs and sustained discussion. Triadic integration rated 'descriptive' because domains are related reciprocally but no specific mechanistic pathways are detailed. BPS typology 'multifactorial' because all domains are substantively present but treated as interacting rather than fully integrated mechanisms.

title: Adopting Principles to Guide Pathways: The Best Model for Geriatric Pain Management
authors: Corey B Simon; Stephanie A. Eucker; Kenneth E. Schmader
pain_condition_detail: chronic pain in older adults, including musculoskeletal pain, neuropathic pain, and pain from multiple chronic conditions
bps_function_set: background framing; explanatory framework; intervention rationale; justification; organizing principle; policy or practice implication
bps_operationalization_summary: The paper uses BPS as an explanatory framework and intervention rationale, describing it as full integration of biological, psychological, and social components. It does not operationalize BPS into specific variables or measures but uses it to justify a set of clinical principles for geriatric pain management.
integration_mechanism_summary: The paper proposes that fear leads to avoidance and deconditioning (bio-psych directional), and that expectations influence treatment outcomes (psych-social directional). It advocates for full biopsychosocial integration but does not specify mechanistic pathways linking all three domains.
conceptual_tensions_1: The paper advocates for full biopsychosocial integration but primarily elaborates psychological factors, with biological and social factors mentioned but not developed
conceptual_tensions_2: The paper uses BPS language extensively but does not specify how the three domains interact mechanistically
additional_observations_1: The paper is a narrative expert review that proposes clinical principles rather than synthesizing empirical evidence
additional_observations_2: The paper emphasizes patient expectations and therapeutic alliance as key psychological constructs but does not use any standardized instruments
additional_observations_3: The paper references the fear-avoidance model and misdirected problem-solving model but does not test or extend them
synthesis_note: This narrative review uses BPS as an organizing framework for geriatric pain management principles but operationalizes it primarily through psychological constructs (fear, avoidance, expectations, self-efficacy, therapeutic alliance). Biological and social factors are mentioned but not elaborated. Integration is partial: directional links between fear and deconditioning, and between expectations and outcomes, but no triadic mechanism.
coding_rationale: Typology is pseudo_bps because BPS language is used extensively but social domain is thin and integration is partial. Triadic integration is partial because bio-psych and psych-social links are directional but bio-social is only mentioned. Psych-dominant balance reflects the paper's focus on psychological constructs.

title: Expanding the Lens: Recent Developments at the Intersection of Pediatric Chronic Pain and Gender Diversity
authors: Allison M. Smith; Megan Silvia; Gwyneth Farr; Hannah Rogan
pain_condition_detail: pediatric chronic pain, with focus on transgender and gender-diverse youth
context_note: U.S.-based review addressing gender-diverse youth in pediatric pain care
bps_function_set: background framing; critique or problematization; explanatory framework; organizing principle; policy or practice implication
bps_operationalization_summary: The paper uses BPS as an organizing framework but argues it is insufficient for TGD youth, instead proposing expanded models that integrate minority stress and ecological systems perspectives.
integration_mechanism_summary: The paper proposes that minority stress and structural adversity affect pain through both biological pathways (HPA axis, inflammation) and psychological pathways (internalizing symptoms, catastrophizing), with social factors like discrimination and healthcare barriers mediating access to care.
emergent_labels_1: gender minority stress and resilience model
conceptual_tensions_1: Tension between gender-affirming care and pain management (e.g., chest binding, hormone therapies causing pain)
conceptual_tensions_2: Tension between individual resilience and systemic barriers to care
conceptual_tensions_3: Tension between psychological distress as both cause and consequence of chronic pain
additional_observations_1: The paper focuses exclusively on transgender and gender-diverse youth, making it a specialized review rather than a general BPS review
additional_observations_2: Biological content is minimal and primarily focused on stress-related biological pathways rather than pain-specific mechanisms
additional_observations_3: The review proposes expanded frameworks (GMSR, ecological systems, intersectionality) to supplement the traditional BPS model
additional_observations_4: There is limited empirical evidence cited, with most studies being small-scale or descriptive
additional_observations_5: The paper emphasizes structural and systemic factors over individual biological mechanisms
synthesis_note: This review examines pediatric chronic pain through an expanded biopsychosocial framework that incorporates minority stress and ecological systems perspectives. It argues the traditional BPS model is insufficient for transgender and gender-diverse youth, who face unique structural barriers and stressors. The paper proposes intersectional, trauma-informed approaches and identifies measurement and access barriers. Biological content is minimal, while psychological and social factors are well-developed. The review is psych-dominant and multifactorial in its typology.
coding_rationale: BPS typology is multifactorial because all three domains are present but biological content is minimal. Integration is psych-social directional with some bio-psych links. TGD focus makes this a specialized review requiring expanded frameworks beyond traditional BPS.

bps_operationalization_summary: The paper uses the BPS label as background framing to justify existential therapy as holistic, but does not operationalize BPS in its methods or analysis. synthesis_note: This scoping review uses the BPS label as background framing to justify existential therapy as holistic, but does not operationalize BPS. It focuses on psychological and existential/spiritual factors, with minimal biological and social content. Integration is limited to directional claims linking existential therapy to pain reduction. The paper contributes to the existential therapy literature but not to BPS operationalization.
coding_rationale: Typology is pseudo_bps because BPS language is used but social domain is minimal and no triadic integration occurs. Triadic integration is 'none' as domains are not related. Psych-dominant due to heavy focus on psychological and existential constructs.

title: Existential therapy for treating chronic pain: A scoping review
authors: Amara Kohlert; Natasha L. Gallant; Taylor G. Hill; Kelsy Dabek
pain_condition_detail: existential therapy for treating chronic pain
bps_function_set: background framing; explanatory framework; justification
bps_operationalization_summary: Positions BPS as explanatory framework for understanding how existential concerns interact with physical and psychological aspects of chronic pain, without specifying mechanisms or operationalizing the model beyond describing it as an interaction between body, mind, and environment.
integration_mechanism_summary: none proposed
emergent_labels_10: combined existential, spiritual, and cognitive‐behavioral treatment method
conceptual_tensions_1: Tension between BPS label usage and complete absence of social domain content
conceptual_tensions_2: Tension between claimed integration of body, mind, environment and actual focus on psychological/existential factors only
conceptual_tensions_3: Tension between theorized mechanisms (pain sensitivity reduction) and lack of specified pathways
additional_observations_1: Review focuses exclusively on existential therapy interventions, not broader BPS applications
additional_observations_2: Spirituality emerges as critical moderator not captured in standard BPS triad
additional_observations_3: CBT integration positioned as necessary complement to existential therapy for physical outcomes
additional_observations_4: All six included studies are RCTs or experimental designs, no purely qualitative BPS analyses
synthesis_note: This scoping review examines existential therapy for chronic pain through a BPS lens but demonstrates pseudo-BPS operationalization: while using the biopsychosocial label and describing interactions between body, mind, and environment, it completely omits the social domain. The review is psychologically dominant, focusing on meaning, identity, death anxiety, and acceptance as psychological constructs, with biological content limited to pain symptoms and sensitivity. Existential therapy is positioned as explanatory framework for reducing pain through unspecified mechanisms, with spirituality emerging as key moderator. The review reveals how BPS language can be used rhetorically
coding_rationale: BPS typology: pseudo_bps - label used but social domain entirely absent. Triadic integration: none - no social domain content. Close call on biological coverage: 'mentioned' rather than 'minimal' due to theorized pain sensitivity mechanism.

bps_operationalization_summary: The paper uses 'biopsychosocial' as a label for multidisciplinary, multimodal care and multidimensional measurement, but never defines the model or specifies how domains interact. integration_mechanism_summary: The paper asserts that PNE reduces fear, which may reactivate descending inhibitory pathways (bio-psych directional), and that physical activity reduces anxiety (bio-psych directional). conceptual_tensions_4: Central sensitization is mentioned as a biological mechanism but not integrated with psychological or social factors in a causal pathway
additional_observations_1: The paper's primary focus is on PNE as an intervention, not on the BPS model itself, BPS is used as a contextual label
additional_observations_2: The review includes parental outcomes but treats them as separate from child outcomes rather than as part of an integrated system
additional_observations_3: The paper recommends combining PNE with exercise and psychological support but does not specify how these components interact mechanistically
synthesis_note: This review uses 'biopsychosocial' as a label for multidisciplinary care without defining the model or specifying domain integration. Psychological content is elaborated (catastrophizing, kinesiophobia, self-efficacy), biological content is mentioned (central sensitization), and social content is minimal. No triadic mechanism is proposed; the paper contributes evidence that PNE improves pain knowledge but does not operationalize the BPS model substantively.
coding_rationale: Typology 'pseudo_bps' because BPS language is used but social domain is thin and no integration mechanism is specified. Triadic integration 'none' because domains are not related to each other in a system. Psych-dominant because psychological constructs and outcomes occupy most of the review.
